title: Machine learning in laser powder bed fusion: a data-centric review of structural prediction and process optimization
abstract: Abstract Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. However, such simulations can also be computationally intensive. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing enables the production of highly complex parts in a cost-effective manner, eliminating the need for assembly of multiple components, and is widely applied across sectors such as the medical, aerospace, and automotive industries [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. As shown in Fig.  1 , AM processes include Vat Photopolymerization (VPP), Material Jetting (MJT), Material Extrusion (MEX), Binder Jetting (BJ), Powder Bed Fusion (PBF), Sheet Lamination (SHL), and Directed Energy Deposition (DED) [ 5 ]. Fig. 1 AM processes according to ASTM committee F42 [ 6 ]

Manufacturing objects using AM involves utilizing a 3D CAD model to build parts by joining or fusing materials layer upon layer, enabling manufacturers to produce geometrically complex components [ 7 ]. Reducing manufacturing time and production costs, minimizing material waste, and enabling the manufacturing of complex geometries are the advantages of utilizing AM compared to traditional processes [ 8 ]. Despite these benefits of AM, several defects still need to be addressed, including the presence of porosity, residual stresses, cracks, and surface roughness, as illustrated in Fig.  2  [ 9 ,  10 ]. The demand for producing different parts with high density, lower porosity and improved design efficiency has driven continuous advancements in the LPBF process [ 11 ]. This process is considered superior to other AM methods due to its ability to create complex geometries with acceptable mechanical properties across a variety of materials and process parameters, resulting in parts with enhanced structural integrity [ 12 ]. Fig. 2 Common defects in AM processes:  a  lack of fusion porosity,  b  keyhole porosity [ 13 ],  c  balling (spattering) [ 14 ],  d  cracking [ 15 ],  e  residual stresses [ 16 ]

During the LPBF process, metal powder is supplied to a build chamber, where the recoater blade evenly spreads a thin layer of powder onto the build plate. Subsequently, the deposited powder is selectively exposed to high-intensity energy generated by a laser, causing rapid melting and solidification, as shown in Fig.  3 . Fig. 3 Schematics of the LPBF process [ 17 ]

The following subsections detail the key process parameters and the inherently highly transient physical phenomena that govern final part quality in LPBF. In the context of a data-driven modeling framework, a thorough understanding of these underlying mechanisms is the critical first step before any data collection begins. Specifically, researchers should establish clear mechanistic relationships among process conditions, thermal history, melt pool dynamics, microstructural evolution, and defect formation to determine which data needs to be collected, particularly when utilizing numerical simulations for data gathering. Ultimately, grounding the data collection process in fundamental physical principles enhances the validity, accuracy, and overall reliability of the trained ML models.

sections.heading: Physical phenomena
paragraphs: The interaction between the laser and the powder bed governs the optical and thermodynamic conditions of the LPBF process. The granular structure of the powder bed promotes multiple internal reflections and scattering of the incident laser radiation, thereby increasing energy absorption compared with a flat substrate [ 18 ]. This interaction is strongly influenced by powder morphology and Particle Size Distribution (PSD), which affect powder spreading, packing density, defect formation, and ultimately the mechanical properties of LPBF components. Metal powders used in LPBF are commonly produced by gas, water, or plasma atomization [ 19 ]. A well-controlled PSD generally improves powder-bed packing, reduces porosity, and contributes to enhanced mechanical performance [ 20 ,  21 – 22 ].

The exceptionally high heating and cooling rates in the LPBF process drive complex micro-scale phenomena, as shown in Fig.  4 . Capillary forces influence melt pool wetting dynamics and spreading behavior; improved wettability can enhance interlayer bonding, reduce lack-of-fusion defects, and contribute to higher final part density [ 23 ]. Additionally, temperature-induced surface tension gradients trigger Marangoni convection, which strongly affects melt pool circulation, heat transfer, solute redistribution, and melt pool geometry [ 24 ,  25 ]. However, excessive energy input can lead to significant metal vaporization, high recoil pressure, and spatter formation. As local cooling reduces recoil pressure, surface-tension-driven capillary forces can destabilize the vapor depression, causing keyhole instability and collapse. This process can trap vapor or gas within the solidifying molten pool, leading to pore formation [ 26 ,  27 ]. Fig. 4 Schematic representation of the physical phenomena occurring along a laser track in the LPBF process [ 28 ]

The complex interplay of these phenomena with the material properties and chemical composition governs melt pool fluid dynamics, rapid solidification, and heat transfer through conduction, convection, and radiation [ 28 ]. Ultimately, these thermo-physical interactions determine the final characteristics of the LPBF components and drive the formation of undesirable defects that compromise mechanical performance. Such defects can significantly affect part quality and reduce mechanical performance under different loading conditions. Therefore, a substantial body of research has focused on elucidating the mechanisms underlying defect formation as a function of process conditions, with the ultimate aim of mitigating or eliminating these defects and improving the mechanical behavior of the parts.

sections.heading: Process parameters
paragraphs: There are several process parameters involved in the LPBF process, and the deliberate adjustment of these variables fundamentally influences the interactions among the complex physical phenomena occurring during printing. Laser power and scanning speed are intricately linked and dictate the total thermal energy delivered to the material. Laser power determines the magnitude of the heat input, while scanning speed controls the laser–material interaction time. Hatch spacing is the perpendicular distance between adjacent laser scan tracks. Proper hatch spacing ensures optimal overlap between melt pools, which is essential for forming a dense, fully consolidated layer. Layer thickness is the depth of the powder spread across the build platform and directly affects the part resolution along the build direction. Thinner layers generally yield superior surface finishes and higher densities but significantly increase total build time [ 29 ]. Scanning strategy, as illustrated in Fig.  5  defines the geometric pattern the laser follows (e.g., continuous raster, stripes, or checkerboard/islands) and the rotation angle applied between successive layers [ 30 ]. Fig. 5 Schematic of different scanning strategies:  a  uni-directional scan,  b  bi-directional/zigzag scan,  c  island scan,  d  variation of scanning sequences based on bi-directional scan,  e  helix scan [ 30 ],  f  chessboard [ 31 ],  g  island scanning strategy using serpentine pattern,  h  island scanning strategy using spiral pattern [ 32 ]

Beyond laser power alone, the physical properties of the laser beam, including focal spot size, wavelength, and spatial energy profile, determine the concentration and spatial distribution of thermal energy. Inert gas flow, defined as the controlled flow of shielding gas, typically argon or nitrogen, across the build chamber, is also critical for process stability because it helps remove metal vapor, spatter, and process byproducts from the laser–material interaction zone [ 33 ]. Preheating, achieved by actively heating the build plate and/or build chamber, reduces the extreme thermal gradient between the localized molten pool and the surrounding material [ 34 ]. Build orientation, defined as the angle at which a part is positioned relative to the build direction or Z-axis, affects nearly every stage of the manufacturing cycle, including support generation, surface quality, thermal history, residual stress development, and mechanical performance [ 35 ].

sections.heading: Defect formation
paragraphs: The complex interaction of thermal phenomena in the LPBF process can introduce defects that significantly compromise the final mechanical performance of fabricated parts. As illustrated in Fig.  6 , several melt-pool-related defects and process instabilities originate from unstable laser–powder interactions, including gas pores, keyhole-induced pores, lack-of-fusion pores, metal vapor, and spatter. These flaws are broadly categorized into porosity-related defects, including lack of fusion, keyhole porosity, and gas porosity; surface and morphological defects, including balling, spatter, and surface roughness; and thermo-mechanical defects, including cracking, delamination, residual stress, and distortion [ 37 ]. Fig. 6 Fabrication defects created during the LPBF process [ 36 ]

Residual stress and distortion are driven by material properties, process conditions, and part geometry [ 38 ]. Defect severity can be further influenced by phase transformations [ 39 ] and thermal properties including thermal diffusivity, heat capacity, and the coefficient of thermal expansion [ 40 ,  41 ]. Consequently, predicting and controlling distortion requires careful optimization of process parameters, including laser power, scan speed, layer thickness, scan strategy, and dwell time [ 34 ,  40 ,  42 ,  43 – 44 ]. Residual stresses develop through three primary mechanisms: tensile stress associated with constrained thermal expansion near the melt pool, compressive stress associated with thermal contraction during cooling (illustrated in Fig.  2 (e)) [ 37 ], and solid-state phase transitions [ 45 ,  46 ]. These internal stresses persist after the build, degrading structural integrity and leading to distortions, dimensional inaccuracies, and cracking [ 47 ,  48 ].

sections.heading: The necessity of incorporating AI/ML
paragraphs: In general, AM has attracted a great deal of attention due to its unique design freedom, enabling the production of highly complex, topology-optimized components across various industrial applications. However, despite these inherent advantages, the widespread industrial adoption of AM, particularly LPBF, remains limited by several persistent challenges [ 49 ]. These include low production rates, stochastic formation of process-induced defects at both micro- and macro-scales, extensive post-processing requirements, limitations in fabricating large-scale components, narrow material compatibility, and a lack of unified computational frameworks capable of linking micro-scale solidification phenomena to macro-scale residual stress and distortion. Over the past decade, significant efforts have been dedicated to addressing these limitations and optimizing the LPBF process through conventional experimental and numerical approaches [ 50 ]. However, these traditional methods are increasingly inadequate for managing the highly coupled, nonlinear, and multi-scale physics that govern LPBF.

Historically, optimization of the LPBF process has relied heavily on empirical, trial-and-error methods. This heuristic approach typically requires repeated printing, sectioning, characterization, and destructive evaluation of physical coupons. Consequently, empirical optimization can incur substantial costs, generate material waste, and consume significant machine time. Furthermore, due to the high-dimensional parameter space of LPBF, experimental methodologies fundamentally struggle to map comprehensive process windows, often converging on locally acceptable conditions rather than globally robust processing regimes [ 51 ]. To bypass the costs of empirical testing, the industry has adopted numerical and analytical approaches, such as Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). However, these deterministic models are often limited by high computational cost. Because the LPBF process is governed by extreme, highly localized multi-physics phenomena, including rapid phase transitions, Marangoni convection, recoil pressure, vaporization, and repeated thermal cycling, developing a high-fidelity model that simulates an entire part from the micro- to the macro-scale remains computationally prohibitive. Simulating merely a few layers of a component can require several hours to multiple weeks on high-performance computing clusters, depending on model fidelity and domain size [ 52 ].

These persistent challenges have motivated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques as complementary tools for process modeling, optimization, and control. The integration of ML frameworks offers important advantages across several critical domains: First, ML-based surrogate models can reduce computational cost by shifting much of the computational burden to the training stage. For instance, while simulating the thermal history of a multi-layer build using traditional FEA may require days on high-performance computing systems, trained deep learning surrogate models can estimate thermal profiles and stress distributions within seconds [ 53 ]. This capability is particularly valuable for accelerating process-window exploration and supporting design-space screening.

Second, AI/ML methods are well suited for inverse design problems. Traditional numerical frameworks, such as CFD and FEA, generally operate as “forward models”: the user inputs process parameters (e.g., laser power and speed), and the model calculates the resulting output (e.g., melt pool dimensions). If an engineer needs to solve the “inverse” problem, namely determining the input parameters required to achieve a desired defect-free or target-quality part, traditional models require numerous computationally expensive iterative simulations. Advanced ML architectures, particularly Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), can learn these complex process–structure–property relationships and substantially accelerate inverse design by reducing the number of required simulations or experiments [ 54 ].

Third, ML enables the integration of heterogeneous and multimodal data sources. Modern LPBF systems are equipped with a diverse array of advanced sensors, generating terabytes of high-frequency optical, thermal, and acoustic data. Traditional deterministic models cannot simultaneously process or ingest these heterogeneous, unstructured data streams. ML models, however, are inherently designed to fuse these distinct modalities, creating comprehensive predictive models that correlate multi-sensor signatures directly to internal part quality [ 55 ].

Finally, ML can support real-time monitoring and closed-loop control. Because conventional mathematical models require hours to process data, LPBF machines have historically operated in an open-loop state, unable to react to real-time process deviations. By evaluating in-situ sensor data and generating defect predictions in milliseconds, ML models eliminate this latency, opening the door to true closed-loop control. Once integrated, an AI framework can detect localized anomalies, such as lack of fusion, excessive heat accumulation, or keyhole instability. This creates the potential for adaptive control strategies, in which process parameters are adjusted during fabrication to reduce defect formation and improve process stability [ 56 ].

While these studies demonstrate the significant advantages of ML in deriving complex process-property relationships, it is crucial to recognize that ML is inherently a data-driven paradigm. Consequently, the predictive accuracy of even the most sophisticated neural architecture is fundamentally governed by the integrity, resolution, representativeness, and physical fidelity of the acquired training data. Therefore, ML algorithms cannot compensate for sparse, biased, or physically inconsistent datasets. This highlights the importance of physics-informed data collection, careful feature selection, and rigorous validation when developing reliable AI/ML frameworks for LPBF.

Recent review studies have examined ML in LPBF from various perspectives, focusing on applications in defect detection, process optimization, and real-time control. Many of these reviews have focused purely on algorithm-centered aspects, classifying ML models used for prediction across different objectives [ 57 ,  58 ,  59 – 60 ]. Some studies have taken a narrower approach, reviewing ML models tailored to specific materials [ 61 ,  62 ] or individual defect types [ 63 ]. Taherkhani et al. [ 64 ] reviewed the integration of ML with in-situ data collection and monitoring systems. Li et al. [ 58 ] presented a lifecycle perspective, organizing ML applications into pre-processing design, in-situ monitoring, and post-processing. Similarly, Liu et al. [ 59 ] provided a comprehensive review of ML applications in LPBF, focusing mainly on algorithm classification and sensing strategies. However, their discussion of numerical simulation workflows as potential data sources was only brief, with limited attention given to the accuracy of modeling strategies or the integration of these simulations within ML pipelines. While comprehensive, their focus is primarily on what methods are applied and where in the process chain, with limited discussion of evaluation practices of datasets.

This review addresses several gaps left by previous surveys: Data-centric perspective: Only a limited number of reviews have examined how ML datasets are collected, particularly with regard to the assumptions underlying data generation for specific LPBF process signatures such as the melt pool, spatter, surface roughness, porosity, microstructure, and residual stress. To address this gap, the present study performs a signature-by-signature evaluation of data-gathering methodologies and simulation assumptions that underpin them. Dataset reliability and domain breadth: This study evaluates the quality and reliability of ground-truth data and highlights risks of simulation-only datasets. It discusses how well these datasets represent real process conditions, how completely they cover the range of process parameters, and how such limitations can reduce the generalization ability of ML models, which are issues that previous reviews have rarely measured or quantified. Actionable guidance: Beyond algorithm selection, this paper serves as a practical roadmap for researchers and practitioners to build more reliable and transparent data-driven frameworks. It offers concrete recommendations and summarizes metrics for designing trustworthy ML datasets, specifically aiding those uncertain about the necessary extent of data collection. The study clarifies the reliability of specific process parameters and critically highlights how foundational assumptions in numerical data generation directly impact the integrity of the resulting datasets.

This study offers a data-centered review that bridges the gap between ML methods and the datasets that enable them. By emphasizing data provenance, dataset quality, and domain coverage, it complements algorithm-based and monitoring-focused reviews, providing a comprehensive reference for developing robust, deployable ML solutions for LPBF.

The structure of this paper is as follows: In Sect.  2 , data acquisition strategies for LPBF are reviewed, including data types, empirical measurements, and simulation-based data acquisition. Specifically, Sect.  2.2  discusses empirical and numerical data acquisition methods across different length scales, highlighting the assumptions and physical phenomena considered in simulation-based data generation. In Sect.  3 , ML models and their applications in LPBF are reviewed, including studies that have employed these models to predict key variables such as melt pool morphology, temperature distribution, defects, and structural/mechanical properties. Section  3.5  focuses on optimizing LPBF process parameters using ML techniques. Finally, Sect.  4  discusses the challenges associated with implementing ML models in the LPBF process.

sections.heading: Data types for ML in LPBF
paragraphs: Data collection forms the foundational stage of any ML pipeline, as the efficacy of a predictive model depends critically on the type, quality, quantity, and representativeness of its training data. Identifying the relevant data types is therefore a prerequisite for selecting an appropriate ML architecture. In the context of LPBF, this task is complicated by the highly heterogeneous nature of available datasets. The process spans a complex matrix of inputs and outputs, ranging from machine-level parameters to transient melt pool dynamics and ultimately to part-level properties such as defect morphology and microstructure, necessitating rigorous data categorization prior to model training. As modern predictive models increasingly adopt hybrid or physics-informed architectures, empirical measurements and their numerical simulation counterparts must be co-registered along a shared process timeline. Accordingly, LPBF datasets encompassing both physical and virtual data modalities are organized into three temporal categories that map the relationship between manufacturing inputs and final part quality: pre-process inputs, in-situ process signatures, and post-process ex-situ evaluations.

sections.heading: Pre-process data
paragraphs: This category encompasses the initial conditions set before the printing process begins. In ML models, these are typically used as the primary independent variables or input features. These include: (a) Process parameters: The controllable machine settings, including laser power, scanning speed, hatch spacing, and layer thickness. These data are almost always tabular and highly structured. (b) Scanning strategy: The toolpath dynamics, such as scan patterns, rotation angles between layers, and part orientation. (c) Feedstock properties: Feedstock properties include PSD, morphology, flowability, and the alloy’s chemical composition [ 65 ]. (d) Simulation-based setup data: In addition to empirical inputs, simulation-generated data are particularly useful because they can be produced under controlled and systematically varied process conditions. By altering inputs such as beam diameter and boundary conditions alongside the aforementioned process parameters, simulations generate structured datasets that support parametric studies before the physical build begins.

sections.heading: In-process data: in-situ signatures
paragraphs: These data are gathered dynamically during the build using sensors, cameras, and acoustic monitors. They capture the complex physics and transient behavior of the process and are often unstructured, requiring significant preprocessing. (a) Thermal history and heat source data: Real-time temperature gradients, cooling rates, and heat accumulation, typically captured via pyrometers or infrared cameras (IR). These data are critical for physics-informed models tracking thermal behavior [ 66 ,  67 ]. (b) Melt pool dynamics: High-speed IR camera imagery capturing melt pool width, depth, length, and shape, as well as spatter generation and plume behavior. This is typically sequential image or video data [ 68 ,  69 ]. (c) Acoustic and optical emissions: Time-series signal data monitoring the acoustic footprint of the laser-material interaction, often used for real-time anomaly detection [ 70 ,  71 ]. (d) Transient virtual signatures: While physical monitoring captures signatures during fabrication, numerical simulations provide an important complementary source of data. Simulations provide access to transient thermal, mechanical, and physical quantities that are difficult to measure directly with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution, such as highly accurate internal thermal gradients, cooling rates, and dynamic melt-pool dimensions.

sections.heading: Post-process data: ex-situ characteristics and outputs
paragraphs: This category represents the final part properties evaluated after the print is complete. In predictive ML models, these metrics usually serve as the target variables (labels) that the model attempts to predict. (a) Macro-scale physical properties: Measurements of relative density, surface roughness, and dimensional accuracy [ 72 ,  73 ]. (b) Defect morphology: Data regarding porosity (e.g., gas pores, lack of fusion, keyhole porosity) and microcracks, often obtained via X-Ray Computed Tomography (XCT) or optical microscopy [ 74 ]. (c) Microstructure and mechanical states: Grain morphology, phase composition, and crucially, the resulting residual stress states and part distortion [ 75 ,  76 ]. (d) Mechanical performance: Traditional mechanical testing results, including yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, fatigue life, and hardness [ 77 ]. (e) Post-processed simulation outputs: Just as physical ex-situ characterization provides ground-truth information after fabrication, post-processed simulation data yield vital predictive outputs. These quantities include heat accumulation, solidification-related descriptors, final residual stress, part distortion, and defect-related indicators. When used as target variables or physics-informed descriptors in ML models, these outputs help expand sparse experimental datasets and greatly improve the interpretability of data-driven models.

While incorporating these virtual datasets is highly beneficial, the reliability of simulation data depends strongly on the fidelity of the underlying numerical model. Assumptions regarding material properties, boundary conditions, heat-source representation, and mesh resolution directly influence the accuracy of the predicted outputs. Therefore, simulation-generated data must be carefully verified and validated against empirical measurements before being deployed in ML model development. For LPBF, researchers must balance computational cost with physical relevance: low-fidelity simulations provide efficient general process trends, whereas high-fidelity models capture detailed melt-pool physics. Ultimately, combining rigorously curated simulation data with empirical measurements reduces dependence on limited physical datasets and enhances the physical consistency of ML predictions. The specific numerical methods used to generate these datasets are discussed in detail in Sect.  2.2 .

sections.heading: Empirical methods
paragraphs: Empirical data acquisition in LPBF can be broadly divided into two complementary strategies: in-situ monitoring, which captures process dynamics in real time during the active build, and ex-situ measurements, which characterize the fabricated part after the build is complete. Together, these two streams produce datasets that are most commonly used in data-driven and ML studies of LPBF.
In-situ measurement:

In-situ measurement involves the continuous acquisition of sensor data during the active printing phase. Because the LPBF process is layer-by-layer and highly transient in nature, these data capture the dynamic laser–material interaction, melt pool evolution, and any process anomalies as they occur. In-situ monitoring has therefore been widely investigated as a foundation for real-time anomaly detection and closed-loop control. It has been heavily researched as a foundation for closed-loop control systems and real-time anomaly detection (Fig.  7 ). The principal methods for in-situ data collection are as follows: High-speed optical imaging:  High-speed cameras, deployed either coaxially with the laser beam or off-axis, are among the most widely adopted tools for in-situ process monitoring. They capture sequential images of the melt pool, vapor plume, and ejected spatter at high frame rates [ 78 ]. Beyond the melt pool itself, high-speed cameras also capture plume dynamics and their interaction with the laser, off-axis high-speed imaging has been used to simultaneously capture the melt pool, plume, and spatters during single-track experiments in LPBF [ 79 ]. Thermal monitoring (pyrometry and IR cameras):  Thermal sensors including single-point pyrometers and area-based IR Cameras are deployed to capture the thermal history of the part during printing. These sensors operate in the visible, Near-Infrared (NIR), Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR), or Mid-Wave Infrared (MWIR) spectral ranges and measure quantities such as peak temperature, melt pool temperature distribution, cooling rate, and Time-Above-Threshold (TOT) metrics. Short-wave infrared thermography has been used as an in-situ monitoring tool to reconstruct the thermal history of LPBF components layer by layer, with extracted thermogram features, including melt pool geometry and cooling rates, serving as inputs to deep learning models for porosity prediction [ 66 ]. Two-color or dual-wavelength pyrometry setups offer absolute temperature measurement by ratioing emission intensities at two wavelengths, partially mitigating emissivity dependence. A coaxial dual-wavelength melt pool temperature measurement system using a single high-speed camera has been developed for LPBF, enabling real-time measurement of temperature distribution, profile, temperature gradient, and cooling rate under varying linear energy densities during single-line printing [ 80 ]. Off-axis IR camera setups provide full-layer thermal maps rather than point measurements, which are particularly useful for detecting heat accumulation, overheating, and layer-level density anomalies. An off-axis IR thermal camera system has been used to monitor the entire slice during PBF-LB/M processing layer by layer, with thermographic parameters correlated to defects such as localized overheating and lack of fusion, validated by micro-tomographic scans of finished parts [ 81 ]. Acoustic emission (AE):  Acoustic emission monitoring captures the airborne or structure-borne acoustic signatures generated by the laser–material interaction, including rapid melting, solidification, defect formation, and keyhole dynamics, as time-series signals. These signals are compact, low-cost, and physically sensitive to volumetric sub-surface events, making them attractive for real-time defect detection [ 82 ]. Optical coherence tomography (OCT)/Inline coherent imaging (ICI):  OCT and ICI are interferometric techniques that provide high-speed, non-contact, sub-surface depth measurements of the keyhole and melt pool surface topology. Unlike cameras or pyrometers, OCT captures actual depth information through coherent light interference, making it uniquely suited for measuring keyhole depth, layer roughness, and surface topology in real time. ICI is a low-coherence interferometric imaging technique that captures high-speed keyhole depth measurements during LPBF, co-axially aligned with the processing laser; keyhole depth directly corresponds to melt track penetration depth and is a key indicator of process quality, with ICI being robust to the intense broadband blackbody and metal vapor emissions that affect simpler optical sensors [ 83 ]. Photodiodes:  Photodiodes are single-point optical detectors that convert incident light intensity from the melt pool region into a time-varying voltage signal, sampled at rates up to hundreds of kilohertz. They offer far higher temporal bandwidth than imaging cameras, making them capable of capturing rapid melt pool fluctuations, laser modulation signatures, spatter emission events, and plume formation dynamics that cameras cannot resolve in real time [ 84 ]. Photodiodes are often deployed coaxially with the laser to track per-scan-vector melt pool intensity variations, and their signals have been fused with imaging data for improved defect detection [ 85 ].
