Ex-situ measurement:

After the build is complete, the finished part is analyzed to determine its physical, mechanical, and structural properties. These measurements provide the ground-truth labels that are most commonly used as target variables in predictive ML models for LPBF. They are divided into non-destructive testing (NDT) and destructive testing. Non-destructive testing (NDT): X-ray computed tomography (XCT):  X-ray CT is one of the most widely used techniques for non-destructive volumetric inspection of LPBF parts. By reconstructing a full 3D digital representation of the internal material from X-ray attenuation data, it enables quantitative characterization of pore size, shape, spatial distribution, and type, distinguishing, for example, between spherical gas pores, irregular lack-of-fusion voids, and keyhole pores [ 86 ]. Surface profilometry:  The as-built surface topography of LPBF parts is characterized using non-contact optical methods, including confocal laser scanning microscopy, focus variation microscopy, coherent scanning interferometry, and structured white light triangulation, as well as contact-based stylus profilometry. These instruments measure surface roughness parameters (Ra, Rz, Sa, Sq) and full areal surface maps [ 87 ]. X-ray diffraction (XRD) residual stress measurement:  X-ray diffraction is commonly used for ex-situ residual stress measurement in LPBF components. By measuring lattice strain from diffraction peak shifts, XRD enables quantification of near-surface residual stresses that develop due to steep thermal gradients, rapid solidification, and repeated thermal cycling during fabrication. These measurements provide important ground-truth data for validating thermo-mechanical simulations and ML models that predict residual stress and distortion. While conventional XRD is generally considered non-destructive for surface measurements, depth-resolved residual stress analysis may require incremental material removal and can therefore be considered semi-destructive [ 88 ]. Destructive testing Mechanical testing:  Destructive mechanical testing provides key ground-truth labels for property-prediction models in LPBF, measuring quantities that directly determine a part’s fitness for service. Standard tensile testing (per ASTM E8 or ISO 6892–1) on dog-bone specimens extracted from LPBF builds yields yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation at break, and Young’s modulus as a function of build orientation, location, and process parameters [ 75 ]. Microstructural analysis:  After sectioning, grinding, and polishing, destructive microstructural characterization provides detailed information on grain morphology, phase distribution, texture, and defect state that is causally linked to the measured mechanical properties. Optical microscopy is used for initial inspection and porosity estimation via image analysis. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) provides high-resolution images of grain boundaries, fracture surfaces, and melt pool boundaries [ 89 ].

sections.heading: Numerical methods
paragraphs: Simulations and numerical methods are employed to optimize AM process parameters by predicting material behavior, thermal effects, and mechanical characteristics, thereby enhancing part quality and process efficiency. As shown in Fig.  8 , these simulations are conducted across multiple length scales, ranging from micro-scale to macro-scale—each capturing different physical phenomena relevant to the LPBF process, as follows: Micro-scale: This scale (in the micrometer range) examines the interaction between the laser beam and powder particles, considering melt pool dynamics and phenomena such as heat transfer, phase changes, melting and solidification at the particle level [ 90 ]. Meso-scale: This scale (from tens to hundreds of micrometers) focuses on the evolution of the thermal distribution, the creation of the melt pool, and the development of thermal stress the behavior across a limited number of powder layers incorporating micro-scale results. It serves as the critical link between the macro-scale and micro-scale capturing localized phenomena that influence overall process behavior [ 52 ]. Macro-scale: This scale (from millimeter to the component scale) assesses the overall thermal and structural behavior, residual stresses and distortion of the entire component including residual stress and distortions, taking into account the cumulative effects of the AM process [ 91 ]. Fig. 8 Schematic of multiscale simulations and their length scales [ 92 ]

Numerous studies have concentrated on micro-scale and meso-scale simulations, developing various numerical methods to investigate the underlying process dynamics in LPBF, which remains a significant challenge due to the complex, multi-physics, and transient nature of the process [ 93 ]. Establishing connections among different length scales is essential for the accurate development of simulation methodologies, ultimately leading to process optimization. The study of processes at the micro-scale and meso-scale is typically conducted together, where all phenomena occurring at the micro-scale for each segment of a layer such as material behavior, melting and heat transfer are integrated within the broader meso-scale context to understand their collective influence on the process. In contrast, macro-scale simulations focus on assessing overall mechanical behavior such as residual stresses and distortion in fabricated components. Over the past decades, research on AM processes has primarily concentrated on multi-scale simulations, incorporating heat source models, inherent strain methods, flash-based thermal and lumped heat source approaches, along with microstructure simulations, to improve process accuracy and optimization [ 28 ].

As illustrated in Fig.  9 , various computational methods are employed to explore the underlying phenomena occurring during the LPBF process across different length scales. The most commonly used approaches include the Discrete Element Method (DEM) for simulating powder dynamics, Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) for modeling melt pool behavior and fluid flow, the Finite-Difference (FD) method for solving heat transfer equations with high computational efficiency, and the Finite-Element (FE) method for analyzing thermal and mechanical responses [ 94 ]. Fig. 9 Numerical approaches for simulating the LPBF process in different scales [ 93 ]  The DEM approach models the interaction of discrete particles or elements, focusing on their motion and interparticle forces. This particle-based method is particularly useful for simulating the behavior of powder particles in the LPBF process, including packing, spreading, and interaction with the laser. DEM is highly suitable for modeling granular materials and particle interactions, capturing the stochastic nature of powder distribution and movement [ 46 ]. Coupled methods can also be utilized to explore the underlying thermal and physical phenomena [ 95 ]. Li et al. [ 4 ] employed DEM to generate random powder bed configurations and coupled it with a CFD model using Volume of Fluid (VOF) method to analyze the interactions between the laser and the powder for the Ti-6Al-4 V material. This coupled approach successfully captured various phenomena, including the formation of the mushy zone (transitional region between the fully liquid and fully solid phases during solidification in metal processing), surface tension effects, the Marangoni effect, laser reflection through ray tracing and recoil pressure. Despite its accuracy in representing powder-level behavior, DEM is computationally expensive due to the need to model individual particles, which imposes significant limitations on the number of particles that can be simulated and requires significant computational resources for large-scale simulations. Consequently, DEM is primarily used for studying the LPBF process in both micro- and meso-scale. Several open-source (such as LIGGGHTS, JAX-AM and GranOO) and commercial software tools (such as Flow-3D) are available, enabling researchers to account for various physical phenomena influencing the process [ 46 ]. Due to the computational limitations of DEM, FE and FD methods are often employed as alternative approaches assuming continuum-based behavior in the laser-powder interaction phase. In these methods, factors such as individual powder particles, powder bed temperature variation, and some other phenomenon such as thermo-fluid behavior are sometimes neglected to reduce the computational time.

FE method is particularly effective for simulating thermal and mechanical phenomena in the LPBF process, including heat distribution, thermal stress and distortion. One of its key advantages is its high accuracy in capturing complex geometries and boundary conditions, making it well-suited for detailed stress–strain analysis and thermal simulations [ 96 ]. Martin et al. [ 26 ] investigated the formation and dynamics of pores in the LPBF process through simulations, utilizing the ALE3D multi-physics software tool, which integrates FEM and FVM approaches [ 97 ]. Their study accounted for the formation and dynamics of pores in the LPBF process by considering fluid flow equations, heat equations, recoil pressure and evaporation cooling. They proposed a novel mitigation technique to minimize pore formation, particularly at the laser beam’s turning points.

The FD method is commonly used for thermal analysis, such as predicting temperature distribution and cooling rates during the process. Its primary advantages include its simplicity and straightforward implementation, as well as its efficiency for problems with regular geometries and simple boundary conditions [ 98 ]. Nevertheless, the FD method is less adaptable to complex geometries and irregular boundaries compared to the FE method, although the FE method is computationally intensive, especially for large and complex models, as it requires fine meshing, which can further increase computational costs. Additionally, it often necessitates finer grid spacing for higher accuracy, leading to increased computational costs.

Integrating these micro-, meso-, and macro-scale modeling approaches offers a comprehensive multiscale understanding of the LPBF process, linking powder-level dynamics to melt-pool behavior and ultimately to the part-scale thermal and mechanical performance of the fabricated component.
Micro scale simulation:

Numerous studies have focused on improving existing 3D heat source models or developing new models to enhance understanding of the heat distribution within the part during the laser scanning in LPBF. For instance, in addition to the original Goldak heat source model, Goldak et al. [ 106 ] proposed another 3D heat distribution with a double-ellipsoidal shape. Their revised power density distribution is considering two ellipsoidal shapes in two orthogonal directions (in-plane directions (not in depth)) since the experimental results showed that considering a steep temperature gradient for the powder region in front of the heat source is not completely accurate. Additionally, it is essential to accurately capture the penetration of the melt pool in the heat source model. Foroozmehr et al. [ 112 ] numerically investigated the optical penetration depth of laser interaction in the powder bed for stainless steel 316L material during the LPBF process. Their model incorporated a 3D-uniform heat distribution while considering the ratio of the effective penetration depth to the Optical Penetration Depth (OPT), providing insights into laser energy absorption and heat transfer within the powder bed. After validating the model against the experimental results, they studied the influence of different scanning speeds on the molten pool dimensions. The study revealed that the molten pool geometry evolves from the beginning to the end of the scanning process, where the size of the melt pool increases progressively from the start to the end of the laser track. In another study, Hasanabadi et al. [ 113 ] introduced a new hybrid heat source model to improve the simulation of the molten pool of metastable beta titanium alloy (Ti-5553) in LPBF process. As illustrated in Fig.  11 , the Gaussian conical heat source model is divided into three distinct regions where each region is multiplied by different coefficients for three sublayers within the powder layer thickness, showing the amount of penetration of the laser energy in each region. Based on the physical observation of powder distribution, they defined this triple-cone heat source with coefficients of 0.9, 0.09, and 0.01 for the first, second, and third sublayer from the top surface of the powder, respectively. This heat source model shows a good agreement with experimental results, with an error of less than 10% in predicting the melt pool dimensions. The commonly used heat source models should also be enhanced as they are typically applicable only within a specific range of energy density. Wu et al. [ 108 ] introduced two novel heat distribution models for the keyhole Plasma Arc Welding (PAW) and analyzed these models using FE method. The study was motivated by the limitations of previous 3D heat distribution models (Gaussian and double ellipsoidal models), which are not suitable for accurately simulating the keyhole PAW process. Although Goldak’s proposed heat source model can simulate the heat distribution in deep penetration welding, it is not capable of accurately representing high-energy density welding processes. Therefore, they defined a new heat source model by defining a new non-linear distribution parameter (Table  1 ). Furthermore, they also modified their conical model to more accurately represent the bulge-like weld configuration of the key-hole PAW. Fig. 11 Triple-cone heat source model defined by Hasanabadi et al. [ 113 ]

Utilizing simulations instead of experiments to capture temperature distribution and melt pool dimensions necessitates a thorough understanding of the underlying phenomena involved in the process. It is essential to consider any assumptions regarding the impact of these phenomena. While several heat source models effectively represent heat distribution, certain conditions with varying process parameters may require modifications to these models. Achieving this adaptability depends on a deep comprehension of the phenomena occurring during the laser track formation.
Meso – macro scale simulation (inherent strain – lumping heat source method):

After completing the micro-scale simulation, the heat source models developed at this scale are used to simulate temperature distribution across multiple tracks and layers at the meso-scale, though only for a limited number of layers. While the micro-scale focuses purely on thermal behavior, the meso-scale includes a detailed both thermal and mechanical analyses, allowing researchers to capture a wider range of physical phenomena that occur during the laser scanning process in LPBF. During this scale, the effect of many process parameters including the layer thickness, scanning strategies, mechanical behavior of the material, and geometry of the part can be simulated. Micro and meso-scale simulations provide valuable information regarding component properties at the level of single or multi-tracks. However, one of the key objectives of the process simulation is to predict mechanical properties such as residual stress and distortion, and applying the meso-scale simulation methods directly to macro-scale simulation is computationally costly, which leads scientists to introduce multi-scale simulation approaches for macro-scale simulation of the AM process.

In the LPBF process, the contraction of upper layers affects the elastic and stress behavior in the lower deposits, a phenomenon that the classical IS method doesn’t account for. Consequently, in order to quantify IS more accurately, the methodology has been refined by incorporating modifications that account for contraction effects known as Modified Inherent Strain method (MIS).

The implementation of the MIS method is based on numerous assumptions, which may introduce errors. Moreover, various parameters such as considering the number of actual layers in a lump layer, different scanning strategies (as shown in Fig.  5 ) where this highly effect the temperature distribution in different direction, geometry of the parts, and process parameters significantly influence the IS values. Without a thorough understanding of these effective parameters, achieving optimal values is not feasible.

The lumping heat source method is another approach enabling researchers to simulate the LPBF process in macro-scale. In this method, lumps of layers are imposed to an equivalent volumetric of heat flux at once, which is capable of deriving residual stresses with low computational cost, as shown in Fig.  13  [ 119 ]. Investigators have been adopting this strategy using different approaches. For instance, a line heat source model can be used where a heat flux is applied to a section of a part at once [ 120 ]. This method is investigated in volume-by-volume, layer-by-layer, hatch-by-hatch, and vector-by-vector [ 121 ]. Imani Shahabad [ 122 ] conducted a multi-track multi-layer thermo-mechanical simulation for determining the residual stress and deformation of cubic parts using line heat source modeling. The results showed that residual stress and deformation have the highest value at the top layer. They also developed a novel effective heat source model by considering a Gaussian profile for the model. The model showed a good performance in predicting the residual stress of parts. Fig. 13 Equivalent heat flux [ 122 ]

In recent years, researchers have employed various approaches, especially simulation methods, to study the behavior of AM processes across different scales. These simulations provide valuable insights into melt pool morphology, temperature distribution, residual stress, and the formation of defects such as pores. Given the multitude of factors influencing these characteristics in fabricated parts, each study aims to deepen the understanding of their individual and combined effects. Additionally, simulation-generated data can be used for training ML models, enabling predictive analysis and optimization of AM processes. However, it’s essential to acknowledge that these simulations rely on specific assumptions, which may impact data accuracy and subsequently affect the performance of ML models trained on such datasets. Therefore, before selecting and applying the ML models, it is crucial to evaluate the procedure of data generation, the importance of process conditions and the accuracy of the generated data. Without this assessment, ML models may fail to effectively optimize the AM process parameters to fabricate products with minimum flaws. Thus, this paper aims to review studies on the application of different ML models with a particular focus on data acquisition methods, the parameters considered for data collection, the input variables considered for the ML models, and the predicted output parameters.

sections.heading: Machine learning (ML)
paragraphs: In recent years, ML algorithms have gained significant attention due to their various applications across industries. Researchers have also leveraged ML techniques to predict features related to melt pools and 3D-printed parts during AM processes, resulting in reduced computational costs [ 123 ]. This paper aims to review recent studies that have utilized ML methods to enhance the understanding of AM processes, with a focus on the ML models employed, the input parameters used for training, the approach to incorporating these parameters, model accuracy, data collection methods, and the overall effectiveness of these models in predicting desired variables. Specifically, the review will address how ML has been employed to predict melt pool morphology, temperature distribution, and common defects and structural properties.

sections.heading: ML models
paragraphs: In recent years, various ML models have been employed to predict a range of mechanical characteristics in AM processes [ 124 ,  125 ,  126 – 127 ]. These models are generally classified into five categories, each comprising specific modeling approaches, advantages, and limitations tailored to specific types of data. In the following, these categories and some of their models are briefly introduced: Supervised learning:  In this category, the models are trained using labeled datasets to map inputs to their corresponding outputs [ 128 ]: Linear Regression (LR):  This method predicts continuous datasets by considering a linear correlation between independent input variables and the target variable [ 129 ]. Logistic Regression:  This method forecasts the probability of binary outputs. This model is used for classification tasks based on some predictor variables [ 130 ]. Decision Tree:  This method is used for prediction of continuous data and classification, splitting the data into several subsets according to the most important features and forming a tree-like structure [ 131 ]. Ensemble Learning:  This technique combines multiple models to improve overall performance, leveraging the strength of individual models [ 132 ]: Random Forest (RF):  This model is an ensemble of some of decision trees. The prediction is made by averaging the results from all the trees, where each tree is trained using a random subset of data [ 133 ]. Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM):  This model is built by connecting multiple models sequentially, where the errors of the previous models are corrected by the next model [ 134 ]. XGBoost:  A model which built by considering regularization for GBM model to prevent overfitting of the model [ 127 ]. Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Support Vector Regression (SVR):  Used for both classification and regression, it finds a hyperplane that creates boundaries among the data, separating them into distinct classes [ 135 ]. Neural Networks (NN):  Consisted of several layers of interconnected neurons or nodes, modeling complicated patterns among data variables [ 136 ]. Unsupervised learning:  Contrary to supervised learning, the outputs are not labeled and the models focus on identifying hidden patterns in the input variables [ 137 ]. K-Means Clustering:  Partitioning the data into several K clusters based on similarity among data, where each data point is assigned to the cluster with the nearest mean [ 138 ]. Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN):  A NN model employs the physical laws by considering equations such as partial differential equations (PDEs) during training. This model has the leverage of being trained with small datasets while achieving high accuracy, making it particularly effective for modeling complex phenomena in AM processes [ 139 ,  140 ]. Reinforcement Learning (RL):  An ML type where an agent interacts with an environment to make sequential decisions, aiming to maximize its cumulative rewards [ 141 ]. Q-Learning:  An approach where the agent aims to maximize future rewards by learning the value of taking certain actions in specific states [ 142 ]. Deep Q-Networks (DQN):  A Q-learning model incorporated with deep neural networks, capable of dealing with large state spaces, allowing the agent to learn from high-dimensional inputs [ 143 ]. Deep Learning (DL):  This approach uses neural networks with a number of layers, which enables the models to create complex patterns in large datasets [ 144 ]. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN):  Mostly used for image processing which can be used for image classification [ 145 ]. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM):  This model is a kind of neural network utilized for processing sequences of data, such as sentences, time series, or any data that has a time component [ 146 ]. Optimization techniques for ML models: Principal Component Analysis (PCA):  A technique for reducing the dimensionality and enhancing the model, reducing large datasets while maintaining significant patterns and trends [ 147 ]. The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (LMA):  This is an optimization technique used to solve non-linear least squares problems. It is particularly useful in curve fitting and training neural networks [ 148 ]. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD):  This is an optimization technique used to minimize a function by iteratively moving towards the minimum using the gradient (slope) of the function. It is particularly popular in training machine learning models, especially DL models [ 149 ]. Kernels:  A kernel is a function used in machine learning, specifically in algorithms like SVM, to transform data into a higher-dimensional space where it becomes easier to classify or regress [ 150 ].

These are the most commonly used models in AM investigations; however, new models have been defined and combined in recent years, reducing errors and providing a better environment for dealing with different types of data, especially small datasets.

As illustrated in Fig.  14 , the comprehensive procedure for developing ML models to predict variables in the LPBF process consists of several key steps: collecting data relevant to the target feature, preprocessing the data to ensure its suitability for model training, selecting appropriate models based on data types and the characteristics of the dataset, testing the models, and enhancing ML performance through continuous monitoring and refinement. The subsequent sections delineate the methodology for each variable in accordance with recent scholarly articles, including the data collection techniques employed, the types of data acquired, the models selected and developed for predictive analysis, and the enhancements integrated into these models. Fig. 14 The procedure of using ML models for prediction target variables in the LPBF process

In the following sections, studies that used ML models to study the melt pool morphology, temperature distribution, and the structural characteristics are covered, and the data sources, and their reliability are discussed. For all the sections, the inputs are grouped and discussed.

sections.heading: ML for predicting melt pool morphology
paragraphs: Studying the AM process for high-quality component fabrication involves determining melt pool dimensions as the first step, especially through process simulation to correlate a heat source model in the simulation. There are three primary melt-pool regimes: (a) conduction, (b) transition, and (c) keyhole, as shown in Fig.  15 . In the conduction regime, relatively low energy density produces a shallow, wide, and stable melt pool that generally results in better material integrity and fewer defects. The transition regime lies between the conduction and keyhole regimes and is characterized by a partially unstable melt pool with mixed features and variable depth and width, depending on the processing conditions. The keyhole regime arises when high laser energy density forms a narrow and deep melt pool, which can enable efficient melting but also promotes instability, gas porosity, defect formation, and cracking [ 23 ]. Fig. 15 Melt pool regimes occur during the laser track named: a Conduction, b Transition, c Keyhole regimes [ 151 ]

Evaluating the melt pool dimensions in the micro-scale also helps assess the quality of the final product. Also, real-time monitoring of melt pool dimensions enables real-time adjustment of the process parameters to reduce defects. However, measuring melt pool dimensions through experiments and simulations can be excessively expensive. To address this challenge, researchers are increasingly employing ML methods, which enable more efficient prediction of melt pool dimensions and allow investigators to optimize parameters more quickly. They have also experimented with different approaches for selecting input variables and the procedure of data gathering, aiming to optimize the performance of these ML models. It is worth noting that in many numerical approaches that use FEM, simulations often rely on the assumption of homogeneous material for the powder, while overlooking the effects of fluid dynamics.

Process parameters, including laser power, scanning speed, beam diameter, hatch spacing, and layer thickness, combine to determine the energy density, which critically impacts part quality and melt pool formation. Nonoptimal energy densities lead to distinct porosity types: excessive energy density causes melt pool instability and high recoil pressure, resulting in keyhole porosity [ 152 ,  153 ], whereas insufficient energy density prevents adequate melting, causing lack of fusion defects [ 154 ]. In the following subsections, studies that use these process parameters to develop ML models are discussed.

sections.heading: Laser power and scanning speed
paragraphs: Laser power and scanning speed should be considered the primary variables influencing the AM processes and melt pool morphology [ 23 ]. Low scanning speed and high laser power strongly influence melt pool dimensions by icreasing energy input. Notably, even at a fixed ratio of laser power to scanning speed, laser power has a more significant impact on melt pool morphology than scanning speed [ 155 ]. Some researchers aimed to find the best models for melt pool dimension prediction for one specific material by considering laser power and scanning speed as the effective parameters of the LPBF process. Kuehne et al. [ 156 ] focused on varying laser power and scanning speed (P = 200–260 W, V = 0.7–1.2 m/s, Lt = 60 um, D = 50 um) to predict melt track geometry in LPBF of Ti-6Al-4V using ML models. They conducted simulations to derive melt pool dimensions using samples generated by FE analysis with a Gaussian heat source model. They trained and compared four ML models: LR, DT, RF, and a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Among the models tested, RF produced the most consistent results for predicting melt pool width and depth. Neglecting most of the complex physical phenomena and using a narrow range of process parameters reduced both the quality and reliability of the ML models developed in this study. However, Wang et al. [ 157 ] incorporated a broader range of process parameters and experimental data, resulting in a more robust and applicable model, while focusing on these same core parameters. They developed a hybrid SVM–DL model to predict melt pool geometries in the LPBF process using NIR thermal imaging. In their study, single-track melt pools were fabricated on a commercial LPBF system using stainless steel material, under various combinations of laser power and scanning speed (P = 125—275 W,V = 400 mm/s—1200 mm/s,Lt = 50 um). For each parameter setting, multiple NIR thermal images were captured to characterize the cross-sectional geometries of the resulting melt pools.

sections.heading: Layer thickness
paragraphs: Layer thickness is another significant variable affecting melt pool dimensions, as highlighted in recent studies. Simson et al. [ 158 ] employed a NN model, supported by experimental data, to predict melt pool morphology in the single-track LPBF process for Inconel 625 material. They fabricated a series of single tracks on a sandblasted SS 304L substrate using different combinations of process parameters. The substrate was cut perpendicular to the single tracks, and they used an optical microscope and ImageJ software to measure specific melt pool geometry characteristics. They considered laser power, scanning speed, and layer thickness as inputs for their NN model (P = 200—400 W, V = 0.02- 0.08 m/s, Lt = 75–125 um), which utilized a back-propagation feed-forward algorithm to forecast melt pool depth, width, and height. Their findings indicated that melt pool depth increases with higher laser power and lower scanning speeds. Notably, while laser power significantly influenced melt pool width, scanning speed had a greater effect on depth. Furthermore, Simson et al. highlighted that layer thickness primarily impacts the height of the melt pool, observing that track width initially decreases as layer thickness increases, before rising due to gravitational effects from the larger melt pool volume. Despite these insights, the limited combinations of parameters, only three in the study by Simson et al., restrict the comprehensiveness of the analyses.

sections.heading: Preheating
paragraphs: Preheating the powder bed is an effective countermeasure, as it minimizes thermal gradients and residual stresses, thereby reducing porosity and enhancing overall density [ 159 ]. To investigate this, Chen et al. [ 160 ] used Flow-3D, incorporating the Marangoni effect, recoil pressure, and buoyant flow to study the effect of preheat temperatures ranging from 100 to 500 °C on an Inconel 718 plate across three melt pool regimes. In the conduction regime, higher preheat temperatures increased melt pool depth and width, transitioning the morphology from semi-circular to an elongated profile and reducing the width-to-depth (W/D) ratio. During the transition regime, both depth and width increased, but the W/D ratio remained stable. In the keyhole regime, depth increased while width initially expanded and then decreased, again resulting in a reduced W/D ratio. Ultimately, melt pool length consistently increased with higher preheat temperatures across all regimes. To incorporate the effect of preheat temperature in data gathering, Baldi et al. [ 161 ] presented a supervised ML approach to predict melt pool morphology in LPBF of Inconel 718 by considering the preheat temperature. The study predicted melt pool depth and width based on key variables: laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness (V = 760–1560 mm/s, P = 190–370 W, Lt = 30–90 um), and build platform temperature (80–170°C). Experimental data were collected from single-track specimens printed under varying conditions using a Renishaw AM500Q machine. They utilized an optical microscope to observe the cross-sections and record the precise geometric measurements of the melt pool depth and width. The authors implemented a regression-based AutoML workflow within the KNIME Analytics Platform to identify the most effective predictive model. KNIME (Konstanz Information Miner) is an open-source, graphical data analytics platform that enables users to design, execute, and manage ML and data processing workflows through a visual interface. KNIME’s AutoML loop evaluates various regression algorithms and the best-performing model is automatically selected [ 162 ]. Eight ML models were evaluated, with gradient boosted trees outperforming others. This performance also significantly exceeded that of Rosenthal’s analytical model, particularly in width prediction. The methodology proved especially effective in capturing the influence of less-studied parameters such as preheating temperature and high layer thickness. They observed that increasing the layer thickness makes the printability region narrower and that increasing the preheating temperature generally makes the melt pool both wider and deeper.

There are additional features including inert gas, beam diameter and hatch spacing that influence melt pool formation, though only a limited number of studies have focused on these parameters using ML. However, considering these factors can enhance the performance of the ML models to some extent and some research have considered these parameters. Rahman et al. [ 163 ] developed an ML framework aimed at predicting melt-pool geometry in the LPBF process using Ti-6Al-4V alloy. The model took five key input features including laser power, scanning speed, laser spot size, layer thickness, and powder porosity and predicted two important output variables: melt-pool width and depth. To build a comprehensive dataset, the authors combined their experimental data, in which melt pool dimensions were measured using SEM, CFD simulation results considering the fluid flow assumed to be incompressible, and values extracted from the literature (P (50—520 W), Lt (58—140 um), V (0–3200 mm/s)). Several ML regression models were tested, including LR, SVM, NN, and various ensemble methods such as RF and Extra Trees. To improve model accuracy, the study applied a range of data processing steps such as normalization, polynomial feature expansion, and synthetic data generation, along with cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning. The Extra Trees model performed best in predicting melt-pool width, while the Gaussian process model gave the most accurate depth predictions. Both showed strong agreement with experimental and simulation data, with less than 1% deviation. A sensitivity analysis highlighted laser power and scanning speed as the most influential factors affecting melt-pool geometry while spot size was one of the less dominant factors. The framework also enabled optimization of process settings, yielding different parameter combinations that maximize melt-pool volume while minimizing energy input. Although it has been noted that incorporating a broader range of features typically enhances model accuracy, the inclusion of certain variables may inadvertently compromise the precision of the ML model. Additionally, the experimental conditions of the data collected from the literature vary, which can impact the performance of the developed ML models since the condition under which such data were extracted may differ.

As demonstrated, incorporating a broader set of process parameters into ML models provides a more comprehensive understanding of melt pool dimensions, ultimately facilitating process optimization and enhanced part quality. Nevertheless, achieving high predictive accuracy requires accounting for additional variables beyond standard process parameters that significantly impact melt pool size.

sections.heading: Geometrical features
paragraphs: In addition to process parameters, particularly those related to energy density, the overall dimensions of a fabricated part can significantly affect process stability. Larger builds require longer scanning durations and more extended thermal cycles, leading to greater heat accumulation and larger temperature gradients. These conditions can increase the risk of lack of fusion defects and residual stresses, which may act as stress concentrators that facilitate cracking, though these effects depend on the material, scan strategy, and LPBF system [ 164 ]. Vaghefi et al. [ 165 ] investigated the effect of geometrical features on the melt pool depth of a stainless steel part produced by the LPBF process using ML models. An MLP-CNN model was trained for depth prediction and various geometries rather than only cubic ones are printed. All the geometries including square, S, L, E, I, H, and step geometries, as shown in Fig.  16 , were fabricated in three layers with four tracks. Laser power, laser speed, and part geometry were the input variables (P = 65–80 W, V = 500–800 mm/s), and the depth of the melt pool was the output for the ML model. They only printed square, step, and S shapes and used microscopy camera attached to an optical microscope to observe the etched cross-sections and measure the melt pool depths and for other geometries they used FEM to derive the melt pool depth. After optimizing the hyperparameters of the model, this MLP-CNN model showed an accuracy of 95% for depth prediction. The most considerable result was that the depth of the melt pool increased for more complicated geometries. While the authors experimentally validated their simulation, physically printing the additional geometries under specific process parameters would have further verified the reliability of their dataset. In another study, Riensche et al. [ 166 ] developed a physics-based ML method to forecast the depth of the melt pool for Inconel 718 components with different overhang geometries with varying heights (21 samples). Using an optical microscope, they measured the melt pool depth of the printed samples. Also, to increase the speed of determining the microstructure evolution of parts, they used an improved method of mesh-free graph theory thermal modeling based on process parameters. The obtained thermal history was used for training the SVM model, using the ratio of velocity to power (P = 200–370 W, V = 670–1250 mm/s), cooling time, and end-of-cycle temperature as inputs and melt pool depth as the output. The thermal simulation model accounts for geometry in generating temperature and cooling profiles. Since temperature and cooling time depend on part geometry, these thermal features indirectly reflect geometric effects. The accuracy of the graph model was validated by in-situ thermal camera measurements with a 3% error. Gaussian SVM is used for the classification of the depth, consisting of 3 different types of depths, and Gaussian SVM Regression is used for predicting the value of melt pool depth. These ML models showed excellent performance in predicting melt pool depths compared to other available ML models. However, in the study by Riensche et al., the temperature-dependent material properties were not considered because of simplicity which can affect the heat distribution and conservation of the energy, lowering the accuracy in determining the melt pool dimensions. Fig. 16 Illustration of printed geometries and their effect on the melt pool [ 165 ]

sections.heading: Material properties and fluid flow
paragraphs: As observed, numerical approaches, commonly used in various studies, are effective for enriching datasets. However, these methods often rely on different assumptions, which can compromise data precision. For instance, numerous studies have employed numerical methods for data generation, often overlooking temperature-dependent variables, properties and effective physical phenomena such as the Marangoni. Nevertheless, these parameters significantly influence melt pool dimensions and should be accounted for to enhance ML model performance. Kumar et al. [ 167 ] employed a feedforward backpropagation type Artificial Neural Network (ANN) architecture-based model with the Levenberg–Marquardt training algorithm to predict the melt pool dimensions of Ti-6Al-4V alloy components in single track LPBF process. By considering the temperature-dependent material properties, 3D Gaussian heat source model, and effective physical phenomena (fluid flow and Marangoni effect), they conducted simulations for various process parameters (power (50–400 W), scanning speed (200–1800 mm/s), and layer thickness (20–100 µm)) to generate data points for training the ML model. Incorporating these physical phenomena provides a better representation of the actual melt pool during the printing process, thereby increasing the accuracy of their dataset. The final ANN model was capable of estimating the width, depth and length of the melt pool with an error below 0.09%. Raihan et al. [ 168 ] also proposed an ML framework for classifying melt pool defects (desirable, lack of fusion, balling, and keyhole conditions) in LPBF. Their hybrid active learning model combines an RF classifier with Least Confidence Sampling to iteratively select the most uncertain data points for labeling, improving classification efficiency. The model was trained using only 150 samples of the dataset of melt pool classes with power, velocity, density, specific heat, thermal conductivity, melting temperature, beam diameter, and absorption coefficient as effective parameters to achieve comparable performance to traditional models trained on 275 samples, with improvements in accuracy and precision.

While previous studies have employed various ML models to predict melt pool dimensions for specific materials, there is significant potential to develop more comprehensive models applicable to a broader range of materials. Akbari et al. [ 169 ] investigated melt pool morphology in metal AM processes, specifically LPBF and Direct Energy Deposition (DED), employing ML algorithms across four types: LPBF, Electron Beam Powder Bed Fusion (EPBF), Laser Based Powder Fed AM process (LDED), and Electron Beam Wire Fed AM process (EDED). They compiled their dataset from published literature and experimental results, training regression and classification models while comparing outcomes against the Rosenthal equation. Initially focusing on power, scanning speed, and beam diameter, they later enhanced their dataset by incorporating material properties. Notably, the inclusion of hatch spacing significantly improved model accuracy. To address the influence of absorptivity on melt pool shape, they utilized two equations for calculating absorptivity [ 170 ,  171 ]. Their study demonstrated that models such as RF, NN, and GB performed exceptionally well, particularly with the addition of absorptivity data. Raihan et al. [ 172 ] further advanced the field by developing a novel sequential learning ML model to predict melt pool dimensions (height, width, and depth). They built upon the dataset gathered by Akbari et al. [ 169 ], employing the SurpriseAF-BO framework and a CTGAN model to address data scarcity. This approach combines two advanced techniques to improve prediction accuracy when data are limited: CTGAN, a model that generates realistic synthetic data to augment small datasets, and SurpriseAF-BO, a sequential learning framework using Bayesian Optimization, where the model learns step-by-step by selecting the most informative data points to improve itself. Together, they form the CT-SurpriseAF-BO model, which learns more efficiently by focusing on valuable data. This innovative approach yielded a CT-SurpriseAF-BO model that outperformed traditional models like RF and SVR, demonstrating the efficacy of sequential learning in improving prediction accuracy. Their input variables included power, laser speed, and beam diameter for depth prediction, while density, melt pool temperature, and thermal conductivity were used for width prediction. This highlights the distinct impacts of different process parameters and material properties on melt pool dimensions. This foundational work set the stage for Mosallanejad et al. [ 173 ], who predicted melt pool depth for 316L, Ti-6Al-4V, and AlSi10Mg materials. They trained their models across various scenarios, starting with laser power and speed, and subsequently integrating material properties like absorptivity, thermal diffusivity, and specific heat capacity. Their findings echoed Akbari et al.’s results, as shown in Fig.  17 , indicating that incorporating diverse features enhances model accuracy, with XGBoost achieving the best performance. According to this, each process parameter and material property affects melt pool dimensions differently. Moreover, they used a model to generate additional training data based on available data. Leveraging insights from the aforementioned studies, these papers indicated that to improve the performance of ML models predicting melt pool dimensions across diverse materials, a comprehensive set of material properties should be considered as input variables. Although collecting data across diverse materials and broad process parameters from different investigations enhances ML model generalizability, inconsistencies in experimental conditions and underlying assumptions among these studies can compromise model reliability. Fig. 17 Improvement in melt pool morphology prediction using additional features for model training, as observed in:  a  [ 169 ], and  b  [ 173 ]

sections.heading: Visualization
paragraphs: Beyond employing ML models for feature prediction, these models can also enhance the demonstration, analysis, and better visualization of derived data from experiments. Zhang et al. [ 174 ] proposed a ML-based framework for determining melt pool morphology in the LPBF process, focusing on both size and shape characteristics. The study utilized experimental data collected from the NIST Additive Manufacturing Metrology Testbed, using Inconel 625 and coaxial high-speed imaging to capture melt pool behavior. An LSTM network was developed to predict melt pool area from build commands (laser power, position, velocity, and direction of laser motion). To complement the numerical size prediction, the authors introduced a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (MP-GAN) that synthesizes realistic melt pool images from the same input features. This approach enabled shape prediction through synthetic image generation, achieving structural similarity. Ellipse regression on the generated images showed that the GAN could capture shape features (e.g., major/minor axes) with up to 92% accuracy. Notably, the synthetic images filtered out spatter and plume artifacts, which increased robustness but potentially limited their realism in capturing certain defects. The integration of LSTM and GAN models demonstrates the feasibility of real-time, image-free monitoring of melt pool morphology based solely on process parameters, offering a cost-effective alternative to sensor-based monitoring. A similar procedure was adopted by Petrik et al. [ 175 ] for melt pool classification. Moreover, Liao et al. [ 176 ] introduced a framework for reconstructing transient 3D melt pool geometries in LPBF using only 2D coaxial melt pool images. The main goal was to enable real-time, in situ prediction and control of melt pool volume. The study focused on LPBF processing of Inconel 625 and relied entirely on a simulation-based dataset. Using finite difference thermal simulations, they modeled a single-layer, multi-track LPBF scenario with time-varying laser power inputs. The simulations yielded high-frequency 3D temperature fields, from which two sets of data were derived: (1) synthetic 2D coaxial images representing the surface temperature distribution, and (2) corresponding 2D depth maps that served as a proxy for 3D melt pool geometry. The melt depth at each (x, y) location was computed by scanning along the z-axis and identifying where temperatures exceeded the solidus threshold. To learn the mapping from coaxial images to melt pool depth maps, the authors trained a U-Net CNN. The model demonstrated strong accuracy in predicting depth.

According to the literature, as shown in Table  2 , several studies have explored various ML models to analyze different melt pool dimensions. Among these models, ensemble techniques such as RF and GB have shown superior performance compared to others. Additionally, it has been observed that using a single ML model for all melt pool dimensions may not be the most effective approach; instead, employing different ML models tailored to each specific dimension can yield better results. sections.heading: ML for predicting temperature distribution
paragraphs: The primary purposes of studying melt pool dimensions in the LPBF process are to understand the density of the printed layers and to develop accurate heat source models for multi-scale simulations. These models enable researchers to predict temperature distributions along the laser scan tracks. Analyzing the temperature distribution is critical for understanding melt pool behavior and allows for accurate assessment of structural responses, such as residual stresses in the fabricated component. Rather than relying solely on numerical and empirical methods to determine temperature evolution, numerous studies have employed ML models to investigate the influence of various process parameters on temperature distribution.

sections.heading: Laser power, scanning speed, material characteristics, and fluid flow
paragraphs: As with melt pool morphology, laser power and scanning speed have been the primary focus of most machine learning studies aimed at determining temperature distribution. Furthermore, because the overall thermal profile of the powder layer is significantly influenced by material properties and fluid flow, these characteristics must also be carefully considered. Hemmasian et al. [ 177 ] developed a CNN model to predict the temperature distribution based on the laser power, speed, and actual process time during single-track laser processing of Ti-6Al-4 V material in the LPBF process. They trained their model using data obtained from simulation results from Flow-3D software, as illustrated in Fig.  18 , enabling them to consider the fluid flow (mass and momentum conservation), evaporation and buoyancy phenomena during the simulation. After validating the results of simulation with experiments, they created three datasets with varying process parameters (power (100–520 W), scanning speed (100–1500 mm/s)) where the powder layers were considered in only one of the datasets. This model was capable of predicting the temperature distribution with great accuracy (RMSE around 5%). Hosseini et al. [ 178 ] also developed two PINN models to predict both temperature distribution and melt pool dimensions for a single track in the LPBF process using Hastelloy-X material. In their investigation, the PINN models were applied to two distinct case studies by solving the heat equation: the first case utilized temperature-independent material properties, while the second incorporated temperature-dependent properties. The model integrated a volumetric heat source within the governing equations, with inputs including spatial coordinates (represented by a non-homogeneous mesh distribution), time, laser power and speed, thermal conductivity, specific heat capacity, laser absorption, and reference density. The primary output of the model was the temperature distribution. The results indicated that the PINN model exhibited exceptional performance in predicting melt pool dimensions and temperature distribution, particularly when compared to FEM results. They also found that factoring in temperature-dependent properties significantly influences the shape of the temperature profiles. Because heat distributes differently as the material’s conductivity and heat capacity change non-linearly, the second PINN was able to provide a much more realistic thermal gradient, allowing them to accurately calculate the actual dimensions of the molten pool. sections.heading: Scanning strategy
paragraphs: Among the process parameters, scanning strategies show a significant impact on the temperature distribution and the choice of scanning strategies significantly impacts temperature uniformity and can create areas with high energy density. In this context, Guirguis et al. [ 179 ] conducted a study on determining the heat accumulation zones using an ML model for the LPBF process of stainless steel 316L . The real-time infrared images derived during the experiments were used to capture these zones over time. The effect of various variables on the heat accumulation spots were investigated including the strip angle (the orientation of the laser scanning path relative to a reference direction) and geometrical features while the laser power, and layer thickness were kept constant and the influence of the heat accumulation spots on the formation of porosity was also studied. The Gaussian SVM with a Gaussian kernel and an ANN model were used and tested for two approaches by considering the real-time data and thermal history data, showing a good performance in predicting these zones especially when using the real-time data. According to their findings, a desired thermal distribution and reducing the heat accumulation spots can be achieved by optimizing strip angle and scanning direction for different geometries. Moreover, these hot spots and pores mainly form on the edges with small angles and small areas. Kozjek et al. [ 180 ] also used an ML model to predict the temperature distribution in the subsequent layer based on the data obtained from the co-axial thermometry measurements of the previous layers. The study kept all process parameters constant except for the hatch and contour speeds. The output variable of interest was temperature. In addition to the toolpath locations and scanning speed, additional input features were considered: solid distribution near the toolpath, laser interaction time, and toolpath direction, which influences the temperature distribution. The effect of part geometry was also taken into account. Data from 15 to 40 layers were found to be appropriate for training the model. An RF regressor was employed and demonstrated good accuracy in predicting the temperature of subsequent layers.

Achieving a uniform heat distribution is critical for minimizing residual stresses and distortions in the LPBF process [ 181 ]. To facilitate uniform heat distribution, it is essential to reduce areas characterized by accumulated heat zones. Qin et al. [ 182 ] employed a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) model for creating scanning patterns in order to have uniform heat distribution during the LPBF process. They introduced a new method for generating paths, containing three options for space movement. The model can either select a path that minimizes the temperature or choose between two of the smoothest paths with the first maintaining a constant laser movement angle. The aim of the model is to find the best path with the lowest amount of energy density derived from simulation, which served as the reward function. They incorporated their path generator framework with an ANN using the deep Q-network which was trained during the generation of the scanning patterns. Other than the scanning patterns, other parameters remained constant, and the distortion was considered as the output for the ML model. Their final DRL model was used to determine the paths for creating polygon shape specimens and four different thin plates. Then, the quality of the parts fabricated by the proposed DRL model showed 47%, 29%, and 17% lower amount of distortion compared to the parts printed by zigzag, chessboard, and ATG patterns, respectively. In another study, Hasan et al. [ 183 ] developed an ML framework to detect overheating anomalies in LPBF using photodiode sensor data. They extracted statistical features (mean, standard deviation, median, quartiles, deciles) from high-frequency signals collected layer-wise during the build process. Four classifiers (RF, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Classifier (SVC)) were trained. To further enhance classification robustness, a Majority Voting Ensemble (MVE) was implemented using the top three classifiers identified via k-fold cross-validation. This ensemble achieved the highest performance overall, outperforming all individual models and previous methods on the same benchmark dataset. Overall, according to the studies, by optimizing the process parameters and the scanning direction, the uniform temperature distribution can be obtained, resulting in the optimal melt pool shapes [ 184 ].

sections.heading: Inert gas
paragraphs: Several other factors influence temperature distribution, but they have been less frequently considered in investigations since they barely change in LPBF. Sharma et al. [ 185 ] investigated the influence of the inert gas on the dynamics of the melt pool in the LPBF process. A Physics-Informed Deep Learning (PIDL) model was used to predict the distribution of the temperature and the velocity of the molten pool and the dataset was generated from simulation. These simulations captured the complex interactions between the inert gas flow, the laser beam, and the resulting melt pool dynamics. They indicated that this PIDL model was capable of predicting the temperature and velocity field using a small size of dataset. Also, they found that considering the boundary conditions has a great influence on the prediction of the model on the velocity profile of the melt pool flow.

sections.heading: Geometrical features and build orientation
paragraphs: Research indicates that part geometry strongly influences localized energy absorption. Furthermore, build orientation, defined as the angle of the part relative to the build platform or build direction, should be considered a key parameter because it directly affects thermal distribution and the resulting part properties [ 35 ]. Alfieri et al. [ 186 ] investigated the impact of build orientation, specifically vertical and horizontal, as shown in Fig.  19 , on the mechanical properties of 17–4 PH stainless steel during the LPBF process. The study involved fabricating cylindrical parts with a diameter of 15 mm, with a total of 30 components printed at various positions on the build plate. Quasi-static tensile tests revealed that the horizontally printed parts exhibited superior tensile strength and strain at maximum load compared to their vertically printed counterparts, aligning with findings from S. Thanumoorthy et al. [ 187 ]. However, the tests also revealed a lower yield strength in the horizontally printed parts, although these differences were not statistically significant.

García-Moreno Caraballo et al. [ 188 ] introduced HotSpot-GCN, a Graph Convolutional Network designed to rapidly identify heat accumulation zones in LPBF designs. The model was trained on a dataset obtained through a hybrid approach combining large-scale FE simulations with small-scale physical validation. First, they simulated compression and 3-point bending tests on 167 digital models (grid, honeycomb, and gyroid structures) to calculate maximum stress, varying the design parameters across specific ranges: external loads (10 to 200 kN), infill percentages (10% to 100%), wall thicknesses (0.5 mm to 10 mm), and infill orientations (the angle of the internal lattice struts) (0° to 90°). Operating independently of material or printing profiles, the network relies exclusively on geometric inputs (such as node positions, boundaries, and area gradients). The model outputs a correspondingly normalized temperature accumulation field bounded between 0 and 1, automatically flagging nodes with predicted values exceeding 0.8 (representing the top 20% of heat accumulation) as critical hotspot zones. Ultimately, HotSpot-GCN achieved a significant computational speedup compared to simplified FEM analyses and proved to be a highly efficient tool for rapid geometric and build-orientation iterations despite producing smoother thermal gradients rather than exact peak temperatures. Fig. 19 Build directions studied in [ 186 ]

Overall, although various experimental techniques exist to measure temperature distributions during experiments, simulation can be used as a viable alternative method to generate data for developing ML models to predict melt pool morphology. However, as indicated in Table  3 , the use of different models to simulate heat distribution, combined with the omission of key phenomena, can compromise data accuracy, thereby reducing the reliability of the resulting trained ML models. Therefore, before using such datasets, it is critical to understand all the effective parameters and assess the dependability of the ML models. Moreover, insights from existing studies suggest that, in order to use the trained ML models, a single model cannot effectively predict all melt pool characteristics such as depth and width or perform consistently across different materials. Also, considering a broader range features for input data can enhance the model performance and these ML algorithms have demonstrated superior prediction compared to the Rosenthal equation in melt pool shape configuration. Nevertheless, there remains a gap in research addressing all the effective parameters on the melt pool shapes. Therefore, the reliability of these defined and trained models is limited to specific range of process conditions.
