sections.heading: ML for the prediction of defects and structural properties
paragraphs: As observed in previous sections, several process parameters affect the melt pool morphology and the temperature distribution, which both contribute to the formation of pores, surface roughness, and residual stress, leading to distortion and cracks and reducing the fatigue life of the fabricated parts, [ 189 ,  190 – 191 ]. The effect of laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness, scanning strategy and the material properties are considered the primary variables influencing the temperature distribution and melt pool morphology and consequently structural behavior of the manufactured parts [ 169 ]. In the following, investigations of different types of defects using ML algorithms are discussed according to the effect of different process parameters.

sections.heading: Surface roughness
paragraphs: Numerous studies have concentrated on surface roughness, recognizing its role in the final features of parts fabricated during the LPBF process [ 192 ]. Consequently, predicting and classifying roughness using ML models can help process optimization, resulting in reduced surface roughness [ 193 ]. While numerical methods for predicting melt pool morphology and temperature distribution are well established, accurately simulating surface roughness remains highly complex and computationally prohibitive. Consequently, empirical data collection, utilizing in-situ process monitoring and ex-situ surface characterization, remains the most reliable and effective approach for gathering accurate surface roughness data, which can be enriched by combining them with numerical results [ 194 ].

Energy density parameters (P, V, Lt, D):  Energy density significantly influences melt pool dynamics and, consequently, the final surface quality of components produced in LPBF. Akbari et al. [ 73 ] predicted surface quality and spatter patterns (spatter velocity and ejection direction) using various ML models, including RF, Gaussian Process Regression, SVM, Regularized Linear Regression, GB Trees, and NN within the LPBF process for four different materials. They compiled a dataset from existing literature, including a wide range of process parameters such as laser speed, laser power, layer thickness, and beam diameter. Additionally, the data were collected from videos of the LPBF process, filtering the melt pool and plume to detect the spatter particles. Among the tested models, the NN outperformed the others in predicting both spatter velocity and ejection direction. Moreover, PCA revealed that increasing laser power correlates with higher ejection velocity, while greater laser speed tends to result in larger ejection angles, highlighting key variables that influence spatter behavior. Following this research, Chebil et al. [ 195 ] also investigated the spatter formation in LPBF by combining DL with traditional computer vision. To better understand this issue, the authors developed a system called SP(AM) 2  (Spatter Analysis Method for AM), which uses high-speed imaging and a YOLOv4-based object detection model to track and analyze spatter in near real-time. YOLO stands for You Only Look Once. It is a family of models that detect objects in images or video frames in a single pass, making it extremely fast and efficient. Their experiments were carried out using a custom-built LPBF setup, where aluminum alloy powder (AlSi10Mg) (made by gas atomization technique) was melted under varying process parameters (P = 100–6500 W, V = 300–1500 mm/s, D = 150–200 um, Lt = 60–120 um). To train the DL model, they first used a traditional computer vision method (MSER) to label over 21,000 images. While MSER provided accurate labels, it missed many spatter particles, especially the smaller ones. This initial dataset was used to train the first YOLOv4 model, which was then refined using a more selective thresholding method. The improved model achieved a high detection rate. The SP(AM) 2  system outputs detailed information about each spatter, including its size, speed, and trajectory. With the data, the researchers were able to show how different process parameters affect spatter behavior. For instance, higher laser power and lower scan speeds produced larger and potentially harmful spatter particles. They also found that scanning overlapping tracks reduced spatter production by about 70%, likely due to reduced powder availability and increased melt pool stability.

Post-processing:  Apart from the process parameters, the post-processing treatments also change the surface roughness of the part. Reddy et al. [ 200 ] explored the application of ML for predicting surface roughness in 3D-printed micro-lattice structures made from A286 steel, produced using LPBF subjected to three typical post-processing treatments: as-printed, stress-relieved, and heat-treated. The authors collected detailed experimental data on surface roughness and micro-Vickers hardness, using a non-contact optical profiling tool, called the RTEC Instruments MFT-5000 Tribometer. Lattice geometry, intermediate roughness, micro hardness measurements, and post-processing conditions were used as inputs to the ML models and nine ML algorithms were compared, ranging from simple linear regressions to more complex methods like RF, SVR, and an ANN. The models were trained and tuned using standard practices as cross-validation and hyperparameter optimization. Among the models tested, RF and KNN stood out for their accuracy and ability to generalize to unseen data.

Labeling data:  Labeling data for training the ML models is challanging as observed in investigations, especially in the study by Chebil et al. [ 195 ] study. To improve this procedure, unsupervised ML models can serve as effective alternatives, as used in the study by Liu et al. [ 194 ] which monitored surface quality in LPBF by combining light scattering with an unsupervised ML model. The main goal was to create a fast, non-contact, and reliable way to detect surface defects during the printing process, without needing to label every possible defect in advance. The authors focused on metal LPBF surfaces and tested their approach using three sample types: one made under optimal conditions (considered defect-free) and two with process variations that led to surface issues. As illustrated in Fig.  20 , to train their model, they simulated how light scatters off a 3D surface using a physics-based model (the Kirchhoff approximation). They measured the surface topography of their specimens using the measuring instrument, Coherence Scanning Interferometer, which captures highly detailed 3D surface topographies. Then, these highly accurate 3D surface models were fed into a numerical simulation to artificially generate light scattering patterns. This allowed them to generate thousands of scattering patterns based on defect-free surfaces with no need for a huge collection of real defect data. The ML model they used was a convolutional autoencoder, which learns to reconstruct the scattering patterns of acceptable surfaces. When it is fed with a new pattern, it tries to reconstruct it; if the surface is very different from the reference, the reconstruction error will be high signaling a possible defect. They validated the method using both simulated and real experimental data. Similarly, Koca et al. [ 201 ] introduced an innovative approach to detecting microscale surface imperfections in LPBF parts by combining light scattering techniques with unsupervised ML. Focusing on Ti-6Al-4V alloy components, the method was designed to identify surface defects such as balling, spattering, and pores smaller than 90 µm, which are often missed by traditional monitoring systems. The process involved shining a 635 nm diode laser onto the surface and capturing the scattered light patterns, which reflect the underlying surface texture. These patterns were analyzed using four different unsupervised ML models: two autoencoders (based on CNN and ANN) and two anomaly detection algorithms (Isolation Forest and Local Outlier Factor). To reduce the need for extensive experimental data, the authors generated synthetic surface data using StyleGAN3, a generative adversarial network trained on real uniform surface measurements. Simulated scattering patterns were then used to streamline the training process. The ML models were trained solely on scattering data from uniform surfaces and then tested on both uniform and defect-containing surfaces from experiments. Among the models, Isolation Forest delivered the best performance, achieving the highest classification accuracy. Tosoratti et al. [ 202 ] also proposed a training-free ML framework for in-situ quality monitoring and defect detection in LPBF. The approach integrates a high-resolution CMOS camera and custom brightfield/darkfield illumination to capture layer-wise images of the deposited layer during the build process. In contrast to conventional ML methods that rely on large, labeled datasets, this method leverages a modified GrabCut algorithm, a graph-based segmentation technique using Gaussian Mixture Models, to extract the geometry of fused parts directly from image data without prior training and labeling the data. In addition to geometry reconstruction, the framework includes unsupervised algorithmic detection of key powder bed defects (recoater strikes, recoater hopping, and lack of powder) using image processing techniques such as adaptive histogram equalization, Gabor filtering, and K-means clustering. This work demonstrates a scalable, interpretable, and cost-effective alternative to deep learning for in-situ monitoring in LPBF, with real-time processing potential and minimal hardware requirements. Overall, experiments must be conducted to collect these data, which can often be impractical. Fig. 20 Spatter recognition procedure used by Liu et al. [ 194 ]

sections.heading: Porosity and part density
paragraphs: The prediction of the porosity facilitates the monitoring of density in fabricated parts. Beyond simply identifying the process parameters involved, the detection and prediction of the locations and causes of porosity defects enable an exploration of the primary reasons for defect formation in components.

Energy density parameters (P, V, Lt, D):  Sah et al. [ 203 ] trained different ML algorithms in predicting the density and porosity defects in the fabricated Inconel 718 parts. They used EOS M290 machine to produce 125 samples by changing the process parameters. The laser power, laser speed, and hatch spacing were considered in the range of 250-350W, 750–1150 mm/s, and 90–130 um, respectively. They measured the bulk density of the printed samples using Archimedes’ principle, and to evaluate porosity and lack of fusion, they used an optical microscope. Their study indicated that the RF model was the best option for predicting the density of the parts, while the KNN model performed best in detecting the lack of fusion. Similar to this study, Taherkhani et al. [ 204 ] considered power (100–200 W), hatch spacing (90–150 um), and laser speed (1000–1500 mm/s) as the effective parameters while taking account the light intensity signal collected by a photodiode for training the SOM model, a Self-Organizing Map (SOM) unsupervised ML model, to predict the porosity of parts fabricated by LPBF. Two separate datasets are employed for training: the first dataset is samples with intentionally induced pores, and the second consisted of samples with randomly pores induced in the parts. The results indicated that this model is able to determine the pores with different shapes and size, even at low power inputs. In addition to these process parameters, Gor et al. [ 205 ] took into account the effect of layer thickness along with laser power, hatch spacing, and scanning speed (P (70–350 W), V (90–1500 mm/s), h (0.975–180 um), Lt (25–40 um)) and investigated the use of ML techniques for predicting the density of stainless steel 316L parts in PBF. The team gathered data from earlier studies. The output was the final density of the SS316L parts. They tested four different ML models: ANN, SVM, KNN, and LR. Among these, the ANN model performed the best, followed closely by SVM. KNN and LR also showed reasonable performance but were not quite as accurate. ANN and SVM were particularly good at handling the complex, non-linear relationships between the inputs and density. Bossen et al. [ 206 ] presented an ML-based approach to predict the relative density of AlSi10Mg parts produced using LPBF. The researchers trained two MLP models using a dataset of samples gathered from the literature [ 207 ], in which relative density was measured optically using micrographs. One model used only process parameters such as laser power, scanning speed, and hatch distance (P (300–800 W), V (1000–2000 mm/s), h (0.1—0.2 mm)), while the other included extra input from FEM simulations of melt pool width and depth. These simulations were validated with experimental melt pool measurements. Both models performed well, achieving less than 1% error in predicting relative density. However, adding simulated melt pool data did not improve the results and slightly increased the error. This was likely due to limitations in the simulation accuracy and the relatively small dataset. Still, the idea of using simulation data is promising, especially for generalizing across different machines or materials.

Material characteristics:  According to the literature, material properties and grain structure significantly influence the formation of pores [ 208 ]. Thus, some studies have enhanced the interpretability of the ML models by incorporating these material-related features into their analysis. Wu et al. [ 209 ] investigated the relative density of martensitic stainless-steel fabricated components in the LPBF process using ML models including RF, KNN, XGBoost, SVM, and Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) models. The collected data were composed of data points from literature considering the material composition, melt pool morphology, laser power, laser speed, layer thickness, beam diameter, hatch spacing (P (180–300 W), V (600–1200 mm/s), h (90–130 um), Lt (30–50 um), D (50–100 um)) as inputs and relative density as parameter for prediction. They found that large hatch spacing leads to the creation of voids in the melt pool while a low amount of hatch spacing is one of the main causes of keyholing during the laser track. Also, GBDT was the best model in predicting the relative density and by employing the SHAP approach, laser power, laser speed, hatch spacing, and beam diameter were considered the most effective variables on relative density.

Geometrical features:  Scime and Beuth [ 68 ] investigated melt pool defects in Inconel 718 fabricated parts in the LPBF process using ML models and Computer Vision (CV) techniques. They employed unsupervised ML and CV to classify experimental data, utilizing features derived from Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), a method used to detect and describe key points in images through a Bag of Words (BoW) approach, which converts a set of image features (like SIFT descriptors) into numerical vectors approach to describe melt pool characteristics, including shape, spatter, and vapor plume. The morphology was categorized into four groups: desirable, balling, under-melting, and keyhole porosity. Experiments were conducted under two conditions named supported and unsupported overhangs to assess the impact of varying thermal conditions, and they mounted a Photron FASTCAM visible-light camera inside an EOS M290 L-PBF machine. The models, trained across various process parameters (P (100–370 W), V (200–1400 mm/s)), indicated that while many melt pools in unstable regimes were linked to keyhole porosity signatures, ‘desirable’ morphologies remained the most prevalent classification under nominal parameters (occurring in 76% of frames). Additionally, it was found that the depth of severe keyholing did not have a controlling influence on the in-situ appearance of the melt pool, and under-melting occurred at low laser power inputs. Significant morphological differences were found between unsupported overhangs and parts printed on bulk geometries, especially at varying distances from the bulk support.

Temperature distribution:  All these features collectively influence the energy density and temperature distribution during laser scanning, which directly impacts the porosity of parts. Therefore, using the temperature evolution of the layers as input to the ML model rather than individually incorporating all influencing parameters can serve as an effective alternative to decrease the dimensionality of input data. This methodology was adopted by Choi et al. [ 210 ] who used a 3D U-Net convolutional NN for predicting the microstructure and lack of fusion of 316L stainless steel. The thermal history of the parts derived from Rosenthal’s equation was considered as inputs, thus the study did not cover keyhole regimes. Porosities including the lack of fusion were predicted using an ML SOM integrated with U-Net CNN architecture, which reduces the dimensionality of the input data and then feeds the reduced data into a U-Net for segmentation tasks in the LPBF process. This framework was formulated to detect the pores without labeling the data by analyzing Optical Tomography (OT) images for different process parameters. Their model is validated by different sets of experiments for intentional and randomized defects. However, while utilizing Rosenthal’s equation to derive the temperature distribution limits the accuracy of the dataset, it accelerates the computation of the thermal history.

In-situ porosity detection:  Similar to data collection for surface roughness, in-situ monitoring for porosity, despite its challenges, offers a promising approach for acquiring reliable and rich datasets. Atwya and Panoutsos [ 211 ] presented a ML framework for in-situ porosity prediction in LPBF, using spectral emissions data. A total of 45 test cubes were fabricated under systematically varied process parameters (P (100—500 W), V (50–300 mm/s)). Spectral emissions were monitored using co-axial photodiodes from the Renishaw InfiniAM system, while porosity ground truth was obtained via high-resolution XCT, capturing several distinct pores. The porosity localization task was approached as a binary classification problem using a range of ML models. The authors introduced a Prior-Guided Neural Network (PGNN), and this approach was compared against NN, SVM, and RF classifiers. Feature extraction was performed on the five closest sensory samples for each defect site, using statistical descriptors of scanning speed, hatch spacing, energy density, and spectral signal intensity. The best-performing model, an optimized PGNN for localizing porosities smaller than 50 µm spherical equivalent diameter (SED), with significant improvements in recall over baseline methods. The PGNN model also demonstrated the ability to localize porosities as small as 38.12 µm SED. As shown in Fig.  21 , Ren et al. [ 212 ] also presented an ML method for real-time detection of keyhole pores during LPBF of Ti-6Al-4V. The researchers used high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging alongside thermal imaging to capture and understand the process in detail. They identified two types of keyhole oscillations, intrinsic (stable and recurring) and perturbative (chaotic and linked to pore formation). To detect the formation of pores, they trained a CNN using time–frequency scalograms derived from thermal imaging data. These scalograms captured distinct frequency patterns associated with each type of oscillation. With in situ X-ray data providing precise labels, the model achieved near-perfect accuracy with sub-millisecond resolution. Moreover, Snow et al. [ 213 ] developed a ML-based framework for in-situ flaw detection in LPBF using high-resolution layerwise imagery. In this work, the authors used Ti-6Al-4V coupons produced on a commercial LPBF system and captured multiple images of each build layer under different lighting conditions. These images were then linked to flaws identified through XCT, which served as the ground truth for training the models. Two types of ML models (NN and CNNs) were tested. The CNNs outperformed NNs across the board, offering higher accuracy and better ability to generalize to new builds. The results showed that the more diverse the training data and the larger the flaws, the better the detection performance. Interestingly, the study found a strong link between larger flaws and the presence of spatter particles captured in the imagery, suggesting that these surface-level features can signal underlying defects. The authors also explored combining outputs from multiple CNNs using an ensemble approach, which further improved accuracy and robustness. Wang et al. [ 214 ] also evaluated integrating multimodal sensing, DL, and closed-loop control to mitigate LPBF manufacturing defects including porosity. The researchers gathered data using an in-situ framework that simultaneously captured acoustic emissions, high-speed optical imagery, and thermal data, supplemented by synchrotron X-ray and eddy current arrays. The collected data and models relied on specific process ranges: 100–400 W laser power, 500–1500 mm/s scanning speed, 20–60 µm layer thickness, and 0.06–0.12 mm hatch spacing, alongside a critical energy-density threshold of 113.6 J/mm 3  energy density threshold to prevent balling. Using these synchronized data and ground-truth labels, they trained an ecosystem of DL models including supervised DNNs, generative MeltPoolGANs, and reinforcement learning frameworks, in an end-to-end manner to automatically extract complex features without manual engineering. Ultimately, these models achieved over 90% accuracy in predicting keyhole porosity and enabled real-time, closed-loop systems to dynamically modulate laser power, effectively suppressing thermal instabilities and improving part consistency.

sections.heading: Residual stress
paragraphs: Another critical defect is residual stress, which significantly influences crack formation, fatigue behavior and distortion of fabricated parts in LPBF. One factor that facilitates the application of ML in predicting residual stress, as compared to previously mentioned defects, is the availability of simulation methods, which can be used for efficient data generation as an alternative to costly and time-consuming experiments. Zhang et al. [ 76 ] proposed a framework for simulating residual stress of five different geometries and mitigating distortion for a cantilever structure fabricated via LPBF using a hybrid approach that integrates simplified FEA and ML. A two-parameter analytical temperature field was employed to drive the mechanical FEA, significantly reducing computational cost while capturing key thermal effects. To generate a robust training dataset, 100 sets of simulations were conducted by varying two key thermal parameters: the peak surface temperature, ranging from 1150 °C to 1500 °C, and a temperature gradient coefficient ranging from 55 to 105. Residual stress data from FEA simulations were used to train three ML models, including MLP, RF, and GB regressors, demonstrating strong predictive performance (R 2  up to 0.98) when validated against experimental measurements. Distortion prediction was also highly accurate, with sub-0.01 mm errors, enabling successful inverse design compensation that reduced geometric distortion in a benchmark part by 94%.

Among numerical methods, the IS and MIS methods are widely adopted for determining residual stress due to its advantages such as lower computational cost compared with full-scale thermo-mechanical simulations. However, it is important to note that these methods also have some associated errors in predicting residual stresses and distortion. Lestandi et al. [ 215 ] proposed a surrogate modeling approach to predict residual stresses in martensitic steel parts produced using LPBF by focusing on the geometrical features. Their study focused on two types of geometries: thin 2D rectangular plates featuring elliptical holes of varying shapes, and 3D wedge-shaped structures. Residual stresses were computed using the MIS method, and these results served as the output data for training ML models. Three different ML approaches were explored: 1. MLP, a straightforward and fast model that performs well on simple geometries but struggles with more complex shapes. 2. a U-Net-based CNN, known for its high prediction accuracy, especially for intricate spatial features, though it requires longer training times. 3. Map-Decompose-Interpolate (MDI), the quickest to train due to its deterministic nature, but generally less accurate, particularly for geometrically complex surfaces. Overall, the U-Net CNN consistently delivered the best performance across most cases, balancing spatial awareness with prediction accuracy. In another study, Dong et al. [ 216 ] also focused on using the IS method to simulate residual stresses in four types of geometries, including circular struts, square struts, thin walls, and combinations with intersections and gaps in martensitic steel parts manufactured using LPBF. The resulting voxel-wise stress data were then used to train a 3D CNN. The model demonstrated strong accuracy in predicting residual stress distributions across different geometries. Additionally, Vulimiri et al. [ 217 ] introduced a DL model designed to determine the residual stress in geometries of various shapes and sizes. They created a dataset of residual stress profiles derived from the Princeton University ModelNet database, utilizing the IS method. The geometries included in their study were the double cantilever beam, the General Electric (GE) jet engine bracket, and GE canonical parts. All geometries were represented as meshes in a uniform voxel grid, and the model was trained sequentially for each slice of the geometry. Based on this dataset, they found that employing a mean–variance estimation Bidirectional Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory NN (BiConvLSTM) was an effective choice. This approach is particularly well-suited for training on sequential datasets. Their model achieved an error rate of only 12% in predicting the residual stress. However, it should be noted that for all the geometries they used the same IS value.

As illustrated in Fig.  22 , the preceding discussion has addressed the use of ML models for detecting typical defects encountered in the LPBF process. It is clear from the Fig.  22  that, given the dataset comprises images captured during experiments, CNN and NN models are among the most suitable and reliable methods available. sections.heading: Fatigue and cracking
paragraphs: After evaluating surface roughness, porosity, and residual stress, these factors, combined with process parameters and geometric features, can be utilized to predict the fatigue behavior of the fabricated part. Li et al. [ 218 ] developed a framework to understand how internal defects affect the fatigue life of parts made from LPBF 17–4 PH stainless steel. The study focused on linking the geometric characteristics of defects, such as their size, shape, and distance from the surface, to how long a part can withstand cyclic loading before failure. Using high-resolution SEM images of fracture surfaces, the authors applied CV techniques to automatically extract detailed defect features. These included classic size metrics (area, perimeter, major/minor axis lengths), shape descriptors (circularity, eccentricity, solidity, angularity), and how close the defect is to the surface. They trained an SVR model to predict fatigue life based on these features. Compared to other ML approaches such as Decision Tree and LASSO regression, SVR gave the most accurate predictions, especially when the data came from samples with consistent heat treatment and testing conditions. Key findings showed that larger defects, those with irregular shapes, and those closer to the surface tend to reduce fatigue life.

Build direction:  Lei et al. [ 219 ] investigated the high-cycle fatigue performance and life prediction of Hastelloy-X fabricated by LPBF. Their work focused on the effect of different build directions on fatigue behavior, aiming to simulate real-world environments, such as those in aerospace applications. The researchers carried out a range of detailed material analyses, including EBSD, TEM, and micro-CT, to gain a better understanding of the development of fatigue damage. These techniques helped reveal key mechanisms, such as dislocation buildup, interactions at grain boundaries, and twin formation. They also gathered a wide set of mechanical and thermal data at different temperatures to feed into their ML models. To predict fatigue life, the team built two types of ML models: an SVM and DNNs. The models used input features including mechanical and physical properties, testing conditions (like stress amplitude and temperature), and the build orientation. The DNN performed best, outperforming both the SVM model and standard S–N curve predictions, showing strong accuracy and generalization.

Post-treatments:  Similar to surface roughness, post-treatments have a considerable impact on the fatigue behavior, which can also be considered. Maleki et al. [ 220 ] conducted a study on the fatigue behavior of fabricated V-notched AlSi10Mg components and subjected the specimens to cyclic loading on a rotating bending fatigue testing machine, examining the effects of various post-treatments using experiments and DL techniques. The treatments investigated included Heat Treatment (HT), Shot Peening (SP), Electro-Chemical Polishing (ECP), and their combinations (hybrid treatments). The study evaluated the effect of these treatments on the microstructure, surface characteristics, and mechanical properties of the components. The findings indicated that HT not only improved the mechanical properties but also reduced the microstructural inhomogeneity. ECP effectively eliminated surface imperfections, while all post-treatments, particularly SP, which had the most significant impact, enhanced the fatigue life of the components. In the context of DL, Maleki et al. used surface modification factor, surface hardness, relative density, and surface residual stress as input variables, with fatigue life as the output prediction variable. Post-treatments were indirectly used in ML by first measuring how they change surface and structural properties. Sensitivity analysis revealed that the surface modification factor and material elongation were the most critical factors influencing the fatigue performance of the parts. Similarly, Wang and Braun [ 221 ] combined a gradient-boosted trees ML model with the SHapley Additive exPlanation framework (SHAP) to evaluate and predict the fatigue lifetime of 316L stainless steel components fabricated by the LPBF process in two different states: as-built and post-treated (The samples were machined and heat-treated with furnace cooling). Moreover, Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) was utilized for determining the correlation between features and the rank of importance of effective parameters are evaluated by SHAP. According to their results, stress amplitude and the mean stress, compared to stress ratio, defect sizes, defect location and as-built/post-treated state, were determined to have the most impact on fatigue performance of the components and post-treatment was found to be a good remedy for decreasing the roughness and residual stress. Furthermore, their model showed good performance in forecasting the number of failure cycles, however, predicting the location of the fatigue failure was not very accurate, requiring more testing data. A more comprehensive study of the effective parameters using ML models was conducted by Centola et al. [ 222 ]. They explored how probabilistic ML techniques can be used to better understand and predict fatigue failures in stainless steel 316L components produced through LPBF. They assembled an extensive training database drawn from published studies. These included details on manufacturing variables such as laser power, scanning speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness, and build orientation, as well as post-processing steps such as thermal and surface treatments. The authors then developed and compared three types of NN models. The first, a Feedforward Neural Network with Likelihood (FFNN-L), provides quick predictions but is limited by the small size of the training data and tends to overfit. The second, a Physics-Informed Neural Network with Likelihood (PINN-L), improves on this by integrating physical knowledge of fatigue behavior into a custom loss function, enabling it to learn from the full dataset, including runout data, with better generalization. However, it is the third model, a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN), that stands out. The BNN generates Probabilistic Stress-Life (PSN) curves at specified reliability and confidence levels, offering a practical tool for safe design under uncertainty. The study is described as “probabilistic” because it does not just aim to predict a single fatigue life value for a given set of inputs. Instead, it aims to model the variability and uncertainty inherent in fatigue behavior. Fatigue life can vary significantly even under identical conditions due to microstructural variations, defects, and measurement variability. Instead of predicting a fixed value (like “one million cycles to failure”), the models predict distributions of possible outcomes, typically represented by PSN curves. This probabilistic approach gives engineers more reliable, safety-conscious design tools, especially for applications where failure is unacceptable (e.g., aerospace, biomedical, nuclear). Also, Cutolo et al. [ 223 ] focused on predicting the fatigue performance of real-world Ti-6Al-4V components. After testing samples built under different orientations and post-processing treatments, they used a GPR model combined with FE-based stress simulations to predict crack initiation and fatigue life. Their framework successfully correlated build features and treatment conditions with fatigue behavior.

Crack:  A novel crack detection method was introduced by Kononenko et al. by integrating acoustic emission signals with ML algorithms [ 224 ]. This method is used for crack detection of parts fabricated via the LPBF process with Al92Mn6Ce2 material. The ML classification models were used for separating the crack AE events from the background noise, using three signal features (standardized moments, waveform, and spectral components) as the basic thresholds for classification. Multiple classification models were trained including logistic regression, Support Vector Classifier with linear (SVC Linear) and squared exponential kernels (SVC RBF), RF classifier, and Gaussian Process Classifier (GPC) with using a k-fold cross-validation procedure as the accuracy determinant. Their results revealed that the GPC model exhibited the best prediction performance among the models. Notably, the choice of signal feature significantly impacted performance. All models exhibited peak accuracy when using spectral components.

sections.heading: Prediction of structural characteristics and mechanical properties
paragraphs: So far, the application of ML models and the methodologies employed for data acquisition in defect detection have been discussed. Nonetheless, the scope of ML can be further expanded to include the prediction of overall structural characteristics such as strength or hardness of components manufactured via AM processes.

Energy density parameters and material characteristics:  Liu et al. [ 225 ] explored the relation among the process parameters, material properties, and structure properties using a GPR model in the LPBF process. They gathered a dataset using a hybrid approach that combined physical fabrication, mechanical testing, microscopy, and thermal simulation. First, they physically printed AlSi10Mg specimens using varying combinations of laser power (150–350 W) and scanning speeds (700–4000 mm/s). They measured the relative density of printed cubes using the Archimedes method and conducted physical tensile tests on dog-bone specimens to extract the mechanical properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation. To gather microstructural data, they sectioned and polished the samples, using SEM and Electron Back-Scattered Diffraction to measure cellular and grain sizes. Finally, to save time on measuring the melt pool for every single sample, they printed a few physical single-scan tracks to calibrate an FEA model, which they then used to rapidly simulate and extract the melt pool width, depth, and ratio for all the other parameter combinations. Laser power, scanning speed, relative density, melt pool depth, width, and the depth/width ratio, grain size, and grain aspect ratio, and cellular size are the input variables to predict the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation. This study showed that their trained GPR model can effectively predict outputs, including unseen data and new process parameters, with high efficiency. In addition, Eshkabilov et al. [ 226 ] developed several ML models to predict the relative density, hardness, yield strength, and tensile strength of 316L stainless steel material for various process parameters including laser power (50–450 W), laser energy density, hatch spacing (0.02–0.1 mm), layer thickness (0.01–0.14 mm) and scanning speed (60–3000 mm/s) for the LPBF process, where the dataset is gathered from the literature. Five different SVM models combined with different kernels including standardized predictors, fivefold cross-validation, a Gaussian kernel function, a radial basis kernel function, and polynomial kernel functions, were evaluated. The SVM models with radial basis and polynomial kernel functions performed best among these models when validated with printed components.

Post-processing:  Wang et al. [ 126 ] broadened the scope of part mechanical-features studies by exploring how annealing influences the microstructure and tensile strength of Ti-6Al-4V alloy produced by LPBF. One of the key challenges in LPBF is that it often results in a brittle martensitic microstructure, which limits the ductility of the printed parts. To address this, the authors systematically annealed samples at temperatures between 300 °C and 950 °C and observed the resulting changes in both microstructure and mechanical performance. Their results showed that annealing at 850 °C for 2 h was particularly effective, as it transformed the brittle phase into a more ductile lamellar structure. This treatment significantly improved the balance between strength and ductility, making the material more suitable for demanding engineering applications. In addition to experimental work, the study also developed an ML model to predict the UTS of the alloy based on process parameters (laser power and scanning speed), annealing conditions, and microstructural features. An MLP was used, and while the model based solely on process parameters performed reasonably well, while incorporating microstructural data, such as grain aspect ratio and α-phase content, boosted prediction accuracy substantially. Shah et al. [ 227 ] also used an ML approach to predict key tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation) of aluminum where chemical composition, processing conditions, heat treatment variables, and grain size were the inputs to the ML. Aiming to ease the trial-and-error burden of experimental alloy design, the researchers assembled a diverse dataset of samples from a wide range of aluminum alloys fabricated through both conventional (casting and wrought processing) and AM methods including LPBF and DED. Each sample was enriched with detailed information on alloy composition, thermal processing, grain size, and calculated elemental properties. The study followed a structured ML pipeline, starting with feature engineering and reduction using PCC and RF feature importance. A variety of regression models were tested, but ensemble methods (particularly GB Regression) stood out. The GB regressor showed excellent predictive performance for yield strength and ultimate tensile strength. The team also used SHAP to identify which features contributed most. For strength predictions (yield strength and ultimate tensile strength), top contributors included the grain size, Zr and Mg content, heat treatment conditions, and atomic radius. For elongation, the model emphasized the roles of Al content, melting point, and embrittling elements like Fe, Cu, and Zn. A highlight of the study was the model’s ability to generalize beyond its training data. It accurately predicted tensile behavior for previously unseen Al–Mg₂Si alloys, showcasing its potential to support alloy development with minimal experimentation.

Geometrical features:  In addition to predicting mechanical properties, ML models also hold significant potential as powerful tools for determining the final geometry of parts and supporting design applications. Asami et al. [ 228 ] took on the challenge of making lattice structure design in 3D printing more efficient and faster. Specifically, they focused on 316L stainless steel parts produced using LPBF. Designing internal structures like honeycombs, grids, and gyroids can be extremely tedious and complex, especially when trying to tailor them for different mechanical loads. To simplify this, the authors turned to ML. They built a dataset from 167 simulated designs, each varying in wall thickness, infill percentage, orientation (the angle of the internal lattice struts), and pattern type. These designs were tested in virtual bending and compression simulations to predict the amount of stress the parts could handle. A few of these designs were also physically printed and tested to make sure the simulations held up in real life. They tested four different ML models including LR, Decision Tree, RF, and GB. The GB model performed best, predicting stress with good accuracy. One interesting takeaway was that the amount of material (infill percentage) and the applied load had the biggest impact on stress. In another study, Peña Corredor et al. [ 229 ] introduced an ML framework designed to predict the thickness of single beads in thin-walled structures, specifically those made from AS7G06 aluminum alloy, with thicknesses ranging from 100 to 450 µm in the LPBF processes. The researchers explored varying laser power and scanning speed. Their approach involved three distinct ML strategies, each with a unique purpose. First, unsupervised K-means clustering was used to group experimental builds based on their thickness and variability. The analysis revealed three distinct regimes related to common defects: balling, keyholing, and stable walls.

Second, a constant-Mean Gaussian Process (GP) model was used. This purely data-driven model predicts wall thickness based on laser power and scan speed. It achieved high accuracy (R 2  = 0.973) and can estimate uncertainty, but requires a substantial amount of data to perform optimally. However, its performance relied on the availability of a relatively large training dataset.

Third, a physically informed Gaussian Process was used. This model incorporates essential domain knowledge through dimensionless parameters derived from thermal models. It infers laser absorptivity during its training. This approach not only enhances prediction accuracy (R 2  = 0.985) but also needs fewer training samples compared to the purely data-driven GP model. Overall, this research highlights how integrating simplified physical principles into ML models can improve interpretability, reduce the need for extensive data, and enhance generalization across different machines and materials. Such hybrid methods are particularly beneficial in AM, where collecting comprehensive data can be expensive and the underlying physical mechanisms are often complex and interconnected.

In addition to previous studies, Thirupathi et al. [ 230 ] proposed a framework to predict mechanical responses, specifically maximum Equivalent Stress (ES) and Total Deformation (TD), in Hybrid Lattice Structures (HLS) fabricated from 316L stainless steel using LPBF. As shown in Fig.  23 , the study introduced a novel hybrid lattice design, which combined two Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) lattice types: one with side diagonal supports and another with side cross supports, forming a layered structure aimed at enhancing load-bearing performance. Different HLS samples were simulated under compression and three-point bending conditions using FEA, with strut diameter and relative density as primary input variables. Three ML models (LR, Decision Tree, and RF) were trained on the simulation dataset to predict ES and TD. Results showed that RF and Decision Tree achieved higher accuracy than LR. To validate the simulations and ML models, 42 physical samples were fabricated via LPBF and tested experimentally. As shown in Table  4 , a variety of parameters influence the overall structural behavior of the printed parts in LPBF. The implementation of ML techniques for determining such behavior is more challenging compared to melt pool morphology and temperature prediction due to the limited availability of numerical approaches. As a result, researchers often resort to extensive experimental data collection. Consequently, processing these data presents significant opportunities, prompting scientists to employ more complex ML models, such as NN and DL models, or to utilize hybrid methods. sections.heading: ML for manufacturing process optimization
paragraphs: This section explores the growing role of ML in optimizing AM and LPBF processes. It examines the use of ML techniques to fine-tune process parameters, reduce defect formation, and enhance part performance with greater efficiency than traditional methods. Additionally, this section discusses various optimization frameworks (such as multi-objective optimization and design space exploration) and evaluates their effectiveness in improving process reliability, repeatability, and scalability in industrial AM applications.

sections.heading: Melt pool morphology and minimizing porosity
paragraphs: One primary goal in optimizing melt pool morphology and minimizing porosity is controlling the energy density, which directly influences melt pool behavior. Key process parameters associated with energy density include laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness, beam diameter, and hatch spacing. Dharmadhikari et al. [ 231 ] utilized a reinforcement learning framework based on Q-learning to optimize the combination of laser power and scan speed, targeting a steady-state melt pool depth, resulting in reduced porosity. Using the Eagar–Tsai model to simulate 3D temperature distribution, they treated the laser as an agent interacting with its environment. Their model identified 888.9 W power and 566.7 mm/s speed as optimal. Similarly, Faizan Mohamed et al. [ 232 ] applied reinforcement learning to minimize porosity in A205 aluminum alloy parts fabricated via LPBF. By integrating the porosity model developed by Liu et al. [ 233 ], which uses dimensionless parameters to predict lack-of-fusion and keyhole pores, their RL-based approach optimized power, scan speed, and hatch spacing. Experimental validation with fixed 30 µm layer thickness showed that the model could effectively recommend parameter sets with only minor deviations. Similar process parameters were also considered in Chernyavsky et al.'s study [ 234 ] which aimed to find the optimized process settings to make high-quality parts without relying on costly and time-consuming trial-and-error. Focusing on AA2024, an aluminum alloy known for its tendency to crack during LPBF, they introduced a Bayesian ML approach for parameter optimization. The team used Bayesian Optimization and a Gaussian Process model. Impressively, the model was able to identify a set of processing parameters that produced defect-free parts with nearly 100% relative density (99.97%). The authors also extended their method to handle bi-objective optimization, targeting both density and build-up rate. Using a more advanced batch optimization strategy, they found new settings that improved speed while still maintaining excellent part quality.

In addition to optimizing process parameters, ML models can also be employed to enhance mitigation strategies for defect prevention and process stability. Mahmood et al. [ 235 ] combined FE simulation with BPNN to generate defect-free process windows for LPBF of Al-357 alloy across different layer thicknesses (30–100 µm). They found that preheating significantly influences defect mitigation: 120 °C and 90 °C were optimal for 30 µm and 50 µm layers, respectively. No preheating solution worked for thicker layers, highlighting process limitations.

sections.heading: Surface roughness and dimensional accuracy
paragraphs: Another important aspect of optimizing the LPBF process through ML techniques involves improving the surface roughness of the fabricated parts. Li et al. [ 236 ] employed a ML approach to find optimized process parameters, especially laser power and scanning speed, while maintaining constant hatch spacing and layer thickness for CoCrMo alloy in the LPBF process. Their objective was to fabricate components with a high relative density of 99% and a low surface roughness of 7 µm. A total of 240 combinations of process parameters were explored to fabricate block samples, using a dataset that included volumetric energy density, laser power, and laser speed to train a GPR model, which is particularly effective with small datasets. The results revealed that merely optimizing energy density does not ensure optimal relative density and surface roughness. Instead, the interplay between laser power and scanning speed is crucial, with a preference for low power and high laser speed to achieve the best outcomes. Additionally, they discovered that laser speed has a greater influence on relative density than laser power. Cao et al. [ 72 ] also reported optimal parameters for LPBF of 316L stainless steel, identifying 232 W power, 800 mm/s scan speed, and 22 µm layer thickness as the best combination for minimizing surface roughness. Similarly, Gu et al. [ 65 ] proposed a generalizable framework to predict relative density and surface roughness using volumetric energy density and a novel non-dimensional energy input feature that incorporates material properties and laser interaction time. Extreme Gradient Boosting (EXGB) performed best among tested models, showing strong accuracy even with limited data and when validated against external datasets from Inconel 718 and Hastelloy X.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: Ultimately, enhancing the mechanical properties of printed parts remains a central objective in the study of the LPBF process. The application of ML models toward this goal has been explored across a range of scenarios: Montalbano et al. [ 237 ] combined a GPR model with Bayesian optimization to efficiently explore and expand the processing space, specifically laser power, scanning speed, and hatch spacing, for LPBF of Ti-6Al-4V. The goal was to identify processing conditions that produce high-density parts with improved mechanical strength. GPR was chosen for its ability to model complex, non-linear relationships between processing parameters and material properties. In this study, porosity, yield strength, and elongation to failure were used as the target variables. The resulting model successfully identified a broader range of viable process conditions that minimized porosity and enhanced mechanical performance. Dong et al. [ 238 ] investigated the distortion compensation method for LPBF by integrating an ML model and the IS method. Their objective was to leverage data generated by IS method to create compensated geometry to achieve lower distortion in final fabricated parts. However, due to the low accuracy and limitations of IS values calculated via simulation, they derived the IS values using an empirical approach. In their study, GPR was used as the ML model, considering the deformation of each point of the geometry obtained from the IS method. According to these scoring variables, the compensated geometry was created from the GPR model. Their model-based compensation method successfully reduced distortion in lattice structures and conical parts by up to 80%. Suzuki et al. [ 239 ] investigated the optimization of LPBF parameters for fabricating WC/Co cemented carbide composites. The main challenge addressed was reducing the formation of a problematic microstructure known as the WC decomposition region, which includes brittle phases that negatively impact mechanical properties. The goal was to increase the proportion of the more desirable WC/Co two-phase region. To do this, the authors combined single-laser scanning tests on sintered WC/Co blocks and full LPBF builds using WC/25 mass% Co powders. They varied key parameters (laser power, scanning speed, and spot size) and analyzed the resulting microstructures using SEM, EDS, and XRD. They trained a CNN model to automatically segment and quantify the WC decomposition areas in SEM images. To improve accuracy, especially for identifying finer WC particles, they included low-magnification SEM images in the training set. The CNN significantly sped up the analysis compared to manual image labeling. To understand the impact of each process parameter on the formation of decomposition regions, the team used Multiple Linear Regression. Laser power had the strongest effect, while scanning speed had the least. These findings were backed by a thermal model simulating how temperature evolves during laser scanning. Additionally, an SVM was used to map out optimal processing conditions that balanced part consolidation with minimal WC decomposition. Parts built using the SVM-recommended settings showed lower decomposition area fractions and improved mechanical performance (e.g., higher hardness and rupture strength) after post-processing, reaching levels comparable to traditionally sintered WC/Co.

This structured synthesis shows how ML enables tailored process optimization across different AM goals from porosity and roughness reduction to fatigue life and distortion compensation. Notably, approaches combining simulation data with experimental validation, and those leveraging advanced ML models like GPR, RL, or CNNs, have shown significant promise in refining LPBF for industrial applications.

sections.heading: Discussions: challenges and perspectives
paragraphs: As observed in the literature, various types of data are utilized for training ML models, depending on the specific aims of prediction, with each type serving distinct purposes. (1) Numerical data are commonly used in regression models and clustering algorithms. (2) Categorical data are typically employed in classification tasks. (3) Image data are utilized for tasks such as object detection. (4) Time-series data, collected at regular intervals, are used in models that predict future values based on historical trends. These data types are organized into two datasets structures that influence the selection and performance of ML models. (1) Labeled data are essential for supervised learning models such as LR, SVM, Decision Trees, and NN. (2) Unlabeled data are commonly utilized in unsupervised learning models such as K-Means Clustering. Moreover, specialized techniques such as SMOTE are necessary for addressing imbalanced datasets [ 196 ]. Moreover, based on the reviewed literature, many studies have focused on enhancing or adapting ML models to better handle the common data challenges in LPBF processes (namely unbalanced, small-sized, or high-dimensional datasets). A notable example is the work of Choi et al. [ 240 ], developed a Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) to predict spatter patterns in LPBF-fabricated parts. Their QCNN outperformed a classical neural network, demonstrating strong predictive capability while using fewer parameters and performing effectively with small and high-dimensional datasets.

It has been shown that based on the specific research objective and the stage of the manufacturing process under investigation, different types of data are gathered and utilized as inputs or outputs in ML models, ranging from pre-build process parameters to real-time in-situ measurements and post-build characterization data. Table  5  provides a comprehensive overview of studies that applied ML to the LPBF process, categorized by the type of input data used and the type of output predicted. The table is organized into nine categories based on the temporal and procedural nature of the data: pre-processing inputs, in-situ inputs, ex-situ inputs, and various combinations of these data types. For each category, the table lists the specific input features and the predicted output quantity. The largest group of studies relies exclusively on pre-processing parameters, primarily laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness, and hatch spacing, to predict ex-situ outcomes such as melt pool morphology, surface roughness, porosity, density, residual stress, and mechanical properties. A smaller but notable set of studies uses pre-processing inputs to predict in-situ quantities such as temperature distribution and melt pool morphology during the build. Studies employing in-situ data alone focus on predicting either real-time thermal fields or post-build defects such as keyhole pores, lack-of-fusion, and cracking. A limited number of studies leverage ex-situ measurements to predict fatigue life. The more advanced categories combine multiple data types; for instance, some studies integrate pre-processing parameters with in-situ sensor data to predict surface roughness and porosity in real time, while others fuse ex-situ and in-situ measurements to model fatigue behavior. The final category brings together all three data types, giving machine learning models a more complete picture of the process and allowing them to predict complex mechanical properties with greater accuracy, reflecting a growing trend toward holistic, multi-source modeling frameworks in the LPBF literature. Developing ML models for studying AM processes requires not only the knowledge of ML algorithms, but more importantly, a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physical phenomena and the effects of process parameters. A clear understanding of how each process parameter influences system behavior is essential for accurate dataset collection and the development of robust ML models that can reliably predict mechanical properties based on specific processing requirements. Without this process-level insight, ML models may risk reduced accuracy and longer prediction times. In this study, the influence of each process parameter on the LPBF process was systematically explored. In addition, the variation in ML model accuracy with respect to the consideration of different process aspects was investigated. Although numerous ML models have been developed and introduced in the literature, a comprehensive ML model that accounts for the full range of process parameters and offers effective alternatives to traditional simulation methods remains underdeveloped. This section highlights the key challenges identified in the reviewed literature and outlines prospective directions for future research. A wide range of ML models has been developed to predict different outcomes in the LPBF process, with each model demonstrating optimal performance for specific predictions [ 72 ,  231 ,  235 ]. The selection and development of an appropriate ML model depends on several factors, such as the dataset characteristics, data type, dataset size, and the number of features considered [ 241 ]. Achieving high prediction accuracy typically requires access to a substantial and diverse dataset. However, in the context of AM processes, collecting extensive experimental datasets remains both technically challenging and cost-intensive. Consequently, many studies have adopted simulation-based data generation as a practical alternative. Although effective in expanding datasets, these methods often rely on simplifying assumptions that may affect the accuracy of the resulting datasets. To reduce the data requirements associated with ML model development, many studies have simplified their analyses by treating certain influential process parameters as constant. While this allows the use of smaller training datasets to achieve improved predictive performance [ 155 ,  179 ,  180 ,  182 ], it may also limit the efficiency and generalizability of the developed ML models. However, in parallel, as noted earlier, efforts have been made to refine or develop ML models specifically tailored to low-data environments [ 168 ]. Notably, specific ML approaches, such as PIDL exhibit inherent robustness to limited data availability and have demonstrated acceptable accuracy under such constraints [ 185 ]. Studies have also shown that incorporating a greater number of features into the training of ML models generally enhances their predictive performance. However, not all features contribute equally, and redundant or weakly influential parameters may unnecessarily increase dataset dimensionality, potentially degrading model accuracy. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the impact of each parameter and, based on its significance, collect and utilize the most relevant data for training the ML models. Figure  24  presents the relative importance of key parameters affecting target variables, as derived from existing literature. The ranking of these parameters is based on their impact on the target variables and the extent to which they can be varied within LPBF systems. Parameters with limited variability, such as inert gas, typically have negligible influence and can be deprioritized during data collection. This figure serves as a practical reference for determining the necessary dataset and identifying which parameters should be prioritized for data collection to maximize model accuracy and process insight. ML models provide a powerful tool for optimizing AM processes, with many studies focusing on identifying process parameters that improve specific output variables. However, the existing literature lacks models that comprehensively capture the full spectrum of predictive requirements in LPBF. Reliable optimization requires an integrated approach that considers all relevant process signatures and their complex interdependencies, supported by robust and comprehensive datasets. Improving one outcome, such as mechanical strength, does not automatically ensure enhancements in others, such as dimensional accuracy, highlighting the limitations of strategies that target individual objectives. This underscores the need for multi-objective, data-driven frameworks capable of balancing performance across multiple outputs. Fig. 24 Relative importance of effective parameters for data collection

This review extends beyond summarizing ML applications in LPBF by systematically examining the data infrastructure underpinning these models. It evaluates how datasets are generated with particular emphasis on the role of simulations in shaping model reliability. Rather than focusing solely on algorithm selection, this review critically assesses dataset fidelity and representativeness, identifies limitations and gaps in current practices and outlines actionable strategies for developing trustworthy, generalizable ML solutions. By reframing LPBF ML research around data fidelity, interoperability, and physics-awareness, this study offers a distinctive perspective that complements and extends previous algorithm-centered reviews.

As discussed earlier, numerous studies have successfully integrated data from numerical simulations with experimental findings. However, the application of developed ML models to generate supplementary data for enhancing these datasets remains underexplored. Additionally, researchers have found that LPBF signatures often exhibit correlations with one another. For instance, several studies have employed relative density to create ML models that predict the mechanical properties of fabricated components [ 220 ,  225 ]. This suggests that by focusing on the development of highly accurate ML models using precise datasets, researchers could generate new datasets that combine data from ML models with experimental and simulation results, thereby enhancing the ability to predict additional target variables. Figure  25  presents this integrated strategy, and suggests this integrated strategy, which holds significant potential for future research endeavors. This diagram highlights the complex multiscale relationships that govern LPBF fabrication outcomes. Key effective parameters such as laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness and preheating temperature, directly influence energy density and thermal behavior, which in turn affect melt pool morphology and downstream mechanical properties. Both experimental data and numerical simulations play critical roles in capturing these interrelated phenomena. Moreover, this framework underscores the necessity of considering all relevant factors, including post-processing treatments and process–structure–property relationships, when training machine learning models aimed at predictive or optimization tasks in LPBF. By pursuing this approach, the pressing need for extensive data generation could be addressed, paving the way for a more holistic strategy in predicting and optimizing the final characteristics of fabricated parts in LPBF. Fig. 25 Direction of developing ML models and generating datasets from ML models, with emphasis on the relationship among effective parameters and variables

Looking ahead, future research in ML for LPBF should increasingly emphasize the development of interoperable, reusable datasets and hybrid modeling frameworks that integrate domain knowledge with data-driven learning. As the field matures, collaborative efforts between material scientists, computational modelers, and machine learning experts will be essential to bridge the gap between simulation fidelity and real-world variability. Ultimately, the advancement of interpretable, physics-informed ML models, grounded in high-quality data and validated across scales, will be pivotal in driving LPBF from experimental optimization to industrial reliability.
